content.text:
Peter Shaw
VP of Investor Relations, Imperial Oil
Good morning, everyone. Welcome to our Q1 Earnings Conference Call. I'm joined this morning by Imperial senior management team, including Brad Corson, Chairman and CEO, John Whelan, President, Dan Lyons, Senior Vice President, Finance and Administration, Cheryl Gomez-Smith, Senior Vice President of the Upstream, and Scott Maloney, Vice President of the Downstream. Today's comments include reference to non-GAAP financial measures. The definitions and reconciliations of these measures can be found in attachment six of our most recent press release and are available on our website with a link to this conference call. Today's comments may contain forward-looking information. Any forward-looking information is not a guarantee of future performance and actual future performance and operating results can vary materially depending on a number of factors and assumptions.
Forward-looking information and the risk factors and assumptions are described in further detail on our Q1 earnings release that we issued this morning, as well as our most recent Form 10-K. All these documents are available on SEDAR+, EDGAR, and our website, so I'd ask you to refer to those. Brad is going to start with some opening remarks and then hand it over to Dan, who is going to provide a financial update, and then Brad will provide an operations update. Once that is done, we will follow with the Q&A session. With that, I will turn it over to Brad for his opening remarks.
Brad Corson
Chairman and CEO, Imperial Oil
Thank you, Peter. Good morning, everybody, and welcome to our Q1 earnings call. I hope everyone is doing well, and it was great to see many of you at our recent Investor Day in Toronto. As you are likely aware, this will be my last earnings call, with John replacing me following next week's AGM and my retirement. Before I leave, I'm really pleased to report another strong quarter for Imperial, with earnings of CAD 1,288 million, which represents an increase of earnings per share by 13% year-over-year and by 6% on a sequential quarter basis. This represents our highest ever Q1 earnings in the company's history. We also generated free cash flow of CAD 1,150 million and ended the quarter with nearly CAD 1,800 million of cash on hand.
That puts us in a very strong financial position. As you may have seen in the release this morning, we intend to renew our normal course issuer bid later this quarter. While there is ongoing volatility in commodity prices, I remain very confident in our ability to grow shareholder value over the long term. Our upstream assets contributed solid production for the quarter, just shy of the record Q1 production we posted a year ago when adjusting for the divestment of XTO Energy Canada. Improved egress continued to support narrower heavy oil differentials than we've seen in the past, and especially during the winter months. This in turn supported our price realizations. Our downstream business delivered once again with strong margin capture in a recovering crack spread environment.
This business continued to benefit from many durable competitive advantages, including integration, proximity to feedstocks, end market, efficient logistics, and our strong market position. Over the next few minutes, Dan and I will detail the results of this strong quarter. Now let's review the Q1 results. As I just noted, earnings for the quarter were CAD 1,288 million, with cash from operating activities of CAD 1,760 million when excluding the impact of working capital. Again, this represents our highest ever Q1 earnings. Now, that sounded so good the first time. I just had to say it again. These results reflect the strength of our integrated business model and our ability to capture value for our shareholders.
In the upstream, we achieved total production of 418,000 gross oil equivalent barrels per day in Q1. Volume was supported by higher year-over-year production at Cold Lake, including continued strong results at Grand Rapids. We also utilized our enhanced winter operating procedures at Kearl to manage through the extreme cold weather conditions in February. Syncrude production was steady year-over-year. In the downstream, refinery throughput averaged 397,000bbls per day, which equates to a refinery utilization of 91%, while petroleum product sales averaged 455,000bbls per day.
Renewable diesel project construction continued at the Strathcona Refinery, and we are on track to start up mid-2025. We paid CAD 307 million in dividends and finished the quarter with nearly CAD 1.8 billion of cash on hand. We remain fully committed to returning surplus cash to shareholders in a timely manner and intend to renew our normal course issuer bid shortly towards the end of Q2. With that, I'll pass things over to Dan to discuss our financial results in more detail.
Dan Lyons
SVP of Finance and Administration, Imperial Oil
Thanks, Brad. Starting with financial results for the quarter, we recorded net income of CAD 1,288 million, up CAD 93 million from Q1 2024, primarily driven by higher upstream margins. When comparing sequentially, Q1 net income is up CAD 63 million from Q4 2024, primarily driven by higher downstream margin capture. Now shifting our attention to each business line and looking sequentially, upstream earnings of CAD 731 million are down CAD 147 million from Q4, primarily due to lower volumes. Downstream earnings of CAD 584 million are up CAD 228 million from Q4, mainly reflecting higher margin capture. Our chemical business generated earnings of CAD 31 million, up CAD 10 million from Q4. Moving on to cash flow.
In Q1, we generated CAD 1,527 million in cash flows from operating activities, excluding unfavorable working capital effects of CAD 233 million. Cash flows from operating activities for Q1 are CAD 1,760 million, up CAD 239 million from Q1 2024. We ended the quarter with CAD 1,764 million of cash on hand. Shifting to CapEx, capital expenditures totaled CAD 398 million in Q1, about CAD 100 million lower than Q1 2024, driven by project timing. Our full-year outlook remains consistent with our previously issued guidance. In the upstream, Q1 spending focused on sustaining and growing production at Kearl, Syncrude, and Cold Lake.
In the downstream, Q1 spending mainly included continued progress on our renewable diesel project at Strathcona. Moving to shareholder distributions. This morning, we declared a Q2 dividend of CAD 0.72 per share, consistent with our Q1 dividend. A reliable and growing dividend remains the foundation of our free cash flow distribution strategy. We also remain committed to returning surplus cash to shareholders. As Brad noted, we intend to renew our annual NCIB share buyback program in June. Now I'll turn it back to Brad to discuss our operational performance.
Brad Corson
Chairman and CEO, Imperial Oil
Thanks, Dan. I know you've all had a chance to look through the numbers, but I do wanna focus your attention on some of our key performance highlights. Upstream production for the quarter averaged 418,000bbls oil equivalent per day. Production was down 42,000bbls per day versus Q4 and down slightly, or 3,000bbls per day versus Q1 2024, which as you may recall, was a record first quarter when adjusting for the XTO divestment, and so off to a strong start for the upstream. We typically do see lower volumes in the first quarter on a seasonal basis versus the back half of the year. In addition, we managed through some extreme cold weather this year in February. Let's move on and talk specifically about Kearl.
Kearl's production in Q1 averaged 256,000bbls per day gross, which is down barrels per day versus Q4 and down 21,000bbls per day versus the Q1 record previously set in 2024. While Kearl got off to a strong start in January, extreme weather conditions rolled in for most of February, conditions we haven't seen since the winter of 2022. We utilized our enhanced operating procedures, including deliberately slowing down volumes, to manage through these extreme weather conditions. I'm happy to report that Kearl materially improved relative to Q1 2022 under similar harsh conditions, when total gross production averaged 186,000bbls per day. That said, we did experience some unplanned downtime in March that impeded a faster recovery.
We managed through that as well, and April was a very strong month, with production very close to our best ever April production record of 300,000bbls per day gross. Despite lower volumes year over year, I continue to be very proud of the Kearl team for their hard work, their resilience, and overcoming adversity, and we continue to have great confidence in Kearl and our plans to grow volumes further and continue to lower the unit cash cost, as you heard us detail at Investor Day. A good example of our continued efforts to optimize Kearl is taking place this month. In May, we're conducting the planned turnaround at the K2 train. The planned turnaround will start next week and is scheduled to be completed by the end of May.
Per our corporate guidance, the expected volumetric impact for the year is around 9,000bbls a day. Following this year's turnaround, we are targeting to run the K2 train for four years, double the previous interval, with the next planned turnaround in 2029. Moving to Cold Lake. For the first quarter, Cold Lake production averaged 154,000bbls per day, which is down 3,000bbls per day versus Q4 2024 and up 12,000bbls per day versus Q1 2024, primarily driven by Grand Rapids and partially offset by production and steam cycle timing. New advantage solvent-assisted SAGD production is enabling transformation at Cold Lake with higher production at lower unit cash costs. Our first quarter results bear that out.
Grand Rapids solvent-assisted SAGD production continued to exceed expectations with a quarterly average production of 23,000bbls per day, supporting Cold Lake's volume, but also improving its unit cash costs, which decreased by over $3 US per barrel compared to a year ago. This is exciting and gives us great confidence in future solvent-assisted SAGD developments, as well as achievement of our production and unit cost goals for the asset. Just last week, we started the planned turnaround work on the Mahkeses plant at Cold Lake. Speaking with the team, the work is progressing well and is expected to be completed by early June, with a full-year volume impact of 3,000bbls a day. The next transformation of the Cold Lake asset is the Leming SAGD project. Construction is materially complete now, with commissioning progressing throughout this quarter.
We are anticipating first steam to be injected this summer, with first production following later in the year. The Leming SAGD project is anticipated to produce an additional 9,000bbls per day at peak levels. I also wanted to provide a brief update on the EBRT pilot at our Aspen lease. We recently reached a key milestone with successful drilling of the three horizontal well pairs. As a reminder, we are constructing the pilot project this year and next, and then intend to start up in early 2027. EBRT is a transformative new technology that could be applied to our significant undeveloped in situ oil sands resource base to achieve low cost, lower emission volume growth for decades to come. Now just a few comments on Syncrude.
Imperial share of Syncrude production for the quarter averaged 73,000bbls per day, which was down 8,000bbls per day versus Q4 2024 and flat versus Q1 2024. During the quarter, as a result of unplanned downtime, Syncrude continued to utilize the interconnect pipeline to import bitumen and gas oil, ensuring the upgrader remained full and producing about 15,000bbls per day, our share of incremental Syncrude Sweet Premium in the quarter. Moving on to the downstream. We refined an average of 397,000bbls per day, reflecting a utilization of 91%. This compares to 407,000bbls per day a year ago and 411,000bbls per day in Q4. Lower throughput in Q1 reflects some additional maintenance conducted in our eastern manufacturing hub.
We're conducting two planned turnarounds here in Q2 at both Strathcona and Nanticoke, as we laid out in our corporate guidance outlook. As a reminder, we have our final planned turnaround at Sarnia later this year, straddling Q3 and Q4. Finally, we expect to complete construction on the Strathcona Renewable Diesel Project facilities shortly here in Q2, with unit startup planned for mid-2025. Petroleum product sales in the quarter were 455,000bbls per day, which is down 3,000bbls per day versus Q4 2024 and up 5,000bbls per day versus Q1 2024. Turning now to chemicals. Earnings in Q1 were CAD 31 million, which was up CAD 10 million versus Q4.
Earnings in the quarter were down CAD 26 million versus Q1 2024, primarily due to lower margins and the aromatic segment shift to the downstream, which we announced effective Q3 of last year. In closing, this was another strong quarter, and I'm very proud of Imperial's positioning for the future. It has been an honor for me to lead Imperial as Chairman, President, and CEO for nearly five and a half years. I could never have imagined that my journey, our journey, would encompass both the most challenging conditions in the company's 145-year history during the pandemic, but then followed by several record-breaking achievements, both operationally and financially, with the best years in the company's history. I am confident that Imperial will continue to thrive and achieve even greater success in the years to come.
I'm also very excited to see our investment decisions coming to fruition, most notably Grand Rapids, that is exceeding expectations, autonomous haul trucks, and other reliability and production enhancements at Kearl. Our Strathcona Renewable Diesel Project that is scheduled to start up in the coming months. These are just a few. From my first day at Imperial, I have been consistently impressed by our team. Over the past five years, I've been continually reminded of the exceptional quality of our people. Their ingenuity, their drive, resilience, and focus are evident every day as they work tirelessly to improve our business and provide critical energy supplies to society. The results of this great team have been reflected in our ability to deliver exceptional shareholder returns, and that commitment remains unchanged.
I'm extremely proud of what we have delivered for our shareholders in terms of share price appreciation, dividend growth, and returning surplus cash through share buybacks. I'm also pleased to welcome John Whelan, who is anticipated to succeed me as chairman and CEO at our upcoming AGM next week on 8 May. As I mentioned at Investor Day, John and I have known each other for over 20 years, and our paths have crossed multiple times. He has worked under my leadership twice during my 42-year career, and we have worked together on multiple leadership teams. John is returning to Imperial after serving as Senior Vice President of ExxonMobil Upstream Company since 2020. Prior to that role, as many of you know, John served as Imperial Senior Vice President for the Upstream from 2017 to 2020.
With his extensive experience, I am confident that John is the right person to lead Imperial into the future. As always, I'd like to thank you once again for your continued interest and support, and wish you all the best in the future. Although I won't be leading any more of these earnings calls, rest assured I will be listening and celebrating the company's continued success. Now we'll move to the Q&A session, so I'll pass it back to Peter.
Peter Shaw
VP of Investor Relations, Imperial Oil
Thank you, Brad. As always, we'd appreciate it if you could limit yourself to one question plus a follow-up so that we can get to all the questions. With that, operator, can you please open up the line for questions?
Operator
Thank you. If you would like to signal with questions, please press star one on your touch-tone telephone. If you're joining us today using a speakerphone, please make sure mute function is turned off to allow your signal to reach our equipment. Again, that is star one if you would like to signal with questions. Our first question will come from Greg Pardy with RBC Capital Markets.
Greg Pardy
Managing Director and Head of Global Energy Research, RBC Capital Markets
Yeah, thanks. Good morning, and look, absolutely great chapter, I think, in Imperial's history. Brad, just all the best to you, and of course, welcome John again. Two very different questions, but maybe just on the operations side, I was curious, the downstream numbers looked, you know, really good, and I know you alluded to some margin capture. I'm just wondering if we could dig in a little bit more into perhaps, you know, where you captured additional margin in the downstream in the Q1 maybe versus others.
Brad Corson
Chairman and CEO, Imperial Oil
Yeah. Thanks for the questions, Greg, and great to hear from you after seeing you at our Investor Day. You know, we talk extensively about the value of our downstream, the value of integration, the advantages we have structurally here in Canada. All of those have contributed to our success here in Q1 in the downstream. Since we got Scott here, you know, maybe I'll ask him to make a few more comments on what's unique here in Q1.
Scott Maloney
VP of Downstream, Imperial Oil
Yeah. Thanks, Brad. We've certainly leveraged a lot of those structural advantages, as Brad mentioned before, to place our barrels in the highest uplift opportunities, both on the eastern and western part of Canada. That's structurally what helped us deliver these stronger numbers this year. We've also had some volatility in the marketplace, and that volatility gives us some opportunity for placing those barrels in the highest uplift opportunities. As you see in typical first quarters, as the quarter goes on, you start to see some maintenance activity from a turnaround perspective start to play in the last part of Q1, and that also enables some additional margin in the downstream business.
Greg Pardy
Managing Director and Head of Global Energy Research, RBC Capital Markets
Okay. Thanks for that. A completely different question. I mean, with the renewal of the NCIB, the last number of years has been, you know, really acceleration into the second half of the year. How are you thinking, especially just given a pretty sloppy oil price backdrop, is the thinking that you'd accelerate or that you would perhaps execute it over a one-year timeframe, or is it all to be determined?
Brad Corson
Chairman and CEO, Imperial Oil
Yeah. It's a great question, Greg. There's no doubt there's a lot of uncertainty in the market. You know, what stands out with this Q1 results is the strong resilience that we provide with the integrated nature of our business model, you know, coupled with just the underlying strength of our assets. That allows us to kind of maintain consistency in our strategies and avoid, you know, having to make fundamental changes. With respect to the NCIB, you know, obviously we're gonna monitor what those external factors are. You know, we're in a very strong cash position right now. We have no reason to believe that's gonna fundamentally change as we move to the second half of the year.
So consequently, you know, we'll be taking the decision as we go as to what's the right pace. As you point out, you know, over the last couple of years, certainly it's been our behavior, our approach to accelerate the NCIB. Really a key driver there is this underlying principle of we wanna return surplus cash to shareholders in a timely manner. Accelerating the NCIB in the past has given us that flexibility. As we look to the future, you know, we'll continue to make those assessments whether that is appropriate or not.
You know, I don't wanna get too far ahead of myself or ahead of, you know, John and the rest of the leadership team, but one of the reasons we've accelerated in the past is to give us flexibility, you know, for an SIB if that was necessary, to further return surplus cash. You know, still a lot of uncertainty several months ahead for the year. You know, what you can count on is we will be returning surplus cash in a timely manner.
Greg Pardy
Managing Director and Head of Global Energy Research, RBC Capital Markets
All right. Thanks very much, and good luck.
Brad Corson
Chairman and CEO, Imperial Oil
Thanks, Greg.
Operator
Our next question will come from Manav Gupta with UBS.
Manav Gupta
Executive Director, UBS
Good morning, Brad. I think a lot of investors would echo that, IMO today is a much stronger company than it was five years ago. I think if you look at the stock price itself, exactly five years ago it was below CAD 21. The stock price appreciation is clearly reflecting the good work that you have put in. My first quick question here is, as we look at... I mean, there's a lot of focus on Kearl cash costs, but if you look at Cold Lake cash costs, again, down about like 18% year-over-year. Now you obviously have Grand Rapids doing better than expected and Leming coming on later in the year. How should we think about the cash cost at Cold Lake for the rest of the year and maybe more importantly for 2026?
Brad Corson
Chairman and CEO, Imperial Oil
Yeah. Thanks for the comment, Manav, and thanks so much for the words and, you know, in recognition of what the whole team has accomplished, you know, which is obviously reflected in our share price, and that has very much been a collective effort of this great organization and team that have surrounded and supported me over the last five years. With respect to your question, I'm glad you called out Cold Lake. You know, we have talked extensively over the last years about Kearl because we've been on an important journey to get Kearl to $20 a barrel. We've achieved that now. We're working quite diligently to get Kearl to $18 a barrel.
What's been progressing in parallel to that is a really important strategy to improve the structural costs at Cold Lake as well. Grand Rapids and, you know, SA-SAGD as a technology is a key enabler because it fundamentally is our lower cost barrels that we're bringing on. You know, as I noted, compared to a year ago, Cold Lake's cash costs are down $3 a barrel, and this is all on our journey, as we talked about at Investor Day, to get us to $13 a barrel. You know, as the year goes on, we're gonna continue to strive for further improvements. Continued Grand Rapids success and strong volume performance will contribute to that.
Then certainly as we start up Leming, you know, those are lower cost barrels as well, and those will further support this journey to $13 a barrel. You know, several months ahead of us, but the strategy is that we are continuing to work on our cost structure really across all our assets, but specifically here at Cold Lake and Grand Rapids, Leming. Everything we're doing with these new developments are targeted towards lower costs. I feel quite good about that. I don't know that there's really anything else I would add at this, but kinda watch this space, 'cause it's really exciting what the team's doing at Cold Lake.
Manav Gupta
Executive Director, UBS
Perfect. My quick follow-up here is, you have a unique refining system. You get your lever to the East Coast crack, Chicago crack, even the West Coast crack. We are in a you know, relatively tougher macro environment, and I just wanted to understand from you, from your refining system, have you seen any signs of recessionary demand kick in? Or the markets you are supplying to, the underlying demand remains relatively resilient even if the macro seems choppy? If you could help us with that.
Brad Corson
Chairman and CEO, Imperial Oil
Yeah, thanks. I mean, I think it is a good question, you know. I think I continue to come back to our resilience. You know, we have a diverse customer base. You know, we have broad infrastructure costs across the country, and all that allows us to take full advantage of the highest value markets that we see. You know, we have not seen any, you know, material degradation in demand. You know, there are always seasonal variations in all of our products, but nothing that I would say is particularly noteworthy at this point.
You know, and then also contributing to that is, you know, when you look at product inventories across the country, you know, not specifically for us, but for the industry, you know, and globally, those inventories are kind of at the lower end of the five-year band. You know, all that contributes to strengthen the marketplace as well.
Manav Gupta
Executive Director, UBS
Thank you.
Brad Corson
Chairman and CEO, Imperial Oil
Thanks, Manav.
Operator
Our next question will come from Dennis Fong with CIBC World Markets.
Dennis Fong
Equity Research Analyst, CIBC World Markets
Hi, good morning. Thank you for taking my questions. I'd like to reiterate my congratulations on a job very well done to you, Brad, and an incremental welcome to John. My first question focuses a little bit on the upstream side. I was hoping you could provide a little bit of incremental data points or clarity that really drive the confidence at running four-year intervals between major maintenance. As well, can you discuss some of the changes in either equipment or operating procedures that allow you for kind of maybe more minor maintenance to be conducted that has, like, moderate or little impacts to output?
Brad Corson
Chairman and CEO, Imperial Oil
Yeah. Thank you, Dennis, and appreciate your comments there at the beginning. It's, you know, it's an exciting journey we've been on with turnarounds at Kearl. You know, when you think about where we were just a few years ago, we were conducting two turnarounds per year, and then moved to one turnaround per year. Now over the last couple of years, we've reduced the duration of each of those turnarounds. You know, and as I mentioned, we're getting ready to start one of those turnarounds here next week, and we, you know, expect to complete it essentially in the same month. Which, you know, historically, we would have never had kind of, you know, turnarounds limited to just 1 month in a year.
As we look to the future, we see this as integral and key to continuing to improve our volume performance and fundamentally our cost performance as well. We are planning after this turnaround to be in a position that we can run much longer between turnarounds, you know, and targeting four years. With that, you know, I've got Cheryl right here. She's right in the middle of this strategy and spent a lot of time with the contractors as they've refined that approach, and demonstrating to her with confidence that this is achievable. Maybe I'll let her talk a little bit about some of the details.
Cheryl Gomez-Smith
SVP of Upstream, Imperial Oil
Sure. Thanks, Brad. As Brad mentioned, we've been on a journey to optimize our turnaround activity. This year, we are spending time to do the work that'll support this further extension to a four-year interval. What's made the difference? What I would say, along this journey, we've been integrating technology, really looking at our data and analytics to make better decisions. We've been benchmarking, continuing to leverage those global learnings. One of the things that you heard during Investor Day is I mentioned that we're sitting on a foundation of a continuous improvement mindset.
Especially when I think about turnaround activity and how we optimize that, it's really focusing on driving clarity and a relentless focus on what needs to be done in a turnaround versus what we can do outside of a turnaround. Those are, you know, there's not a single item there. It's a mix of all of those enablers that are really gonna get us from where we are right now to this four-year interval.
Dennis Fong
Equity Research Analyst, CIBC World Markets
Great. I really appreciate that incremental clarity. My second question here is maybe targeted to Brad and maybe John. Through time, Imperial has acted opportunistically and even countercyclically in terms of spending or deploying capital, especially as compared to some of your peers. Given the combination of the balance sheet strength that you see today, the longer duration of view that Imperial takes on investment cycles, how are you strategically thinking about potentially taking advantage of all the uncertainty we see today in the market?
Brad Corson
Chairman and CEO, Imperial Oil
Yeah. Thanks for that question. You know, certainly that has our strategy in the past of ensuring that we are optimizing our capital, you know, how we target specific projects and, you know, really focused on highest return. I take that part of your underlying question is really about M&A type opportunities. As I mentioned in the past, you know, the aperture has always been open and, you know. The bar is high because, you know, we have a very high-quality portfolio today. Anything we would pursue would have to compete with that. You know, I don't expect that's gonna fundamentally change. John is here, and he'll be kind of steering the ship now in the future. Maybe I'll let him talk a little bit about that.
John Whelan
President, Imperial Oil
Yeah. Thanks, Brad. No, and I think it will not fundamentally change. I think, you know, first, maybe I should say, you know, I'm really humbled and excited to return to Imperial in this role. As a Canadian, you know, to have the opportunity to lead this company with such a long, proud Canadian history of over 145 years. You know, truly is an honor. I also, I would echo many of the comments that were in the questions and opening remarks today, that I recognize I have some really big shoes to fill coming in behind Brad. As he's mentioned, we've known each other for over 20 years, and I know what a great leader and a great person he is.
Imperial's performance under Brad has been outstanding, and I'm committed to making sure that we continue that outstanding performance going forward. I'm committed to ensuring our shareholders, stakeholders, and employees are proud to be a part of and associated with this company. What you'll see under my leadership, you know, Imperial strategy to win will remain very consistent, and it's really about increasing cash flow and delivering unmatched industry-leading shareholder returns. That focus will be the same. It'll be on maximizing the value of our existing assets, you know, targeted optimization and continued structural cost improvements. It's gonna be investing on select growth opportunities within those assets, like enhancements at Kearl and Cold Lake and Strathcona.
Progressing some future strategic growth, you know, when we think about our in-situ business and continuing to assess opportunities as the energy transition landscape evolves, utilizing technology and so on to take advantage of that and our relationship with ExxonMobil. You'll see a very consistent strategy, which I think has been a successful strategy as we go forward. I'll be working very hard to leverage our competitive advantages, and I think we have advantages that others do not have around technology, around scale, integration, execution excellence, doing the right thing the right way to a high standard each and every time. What Brad talked about, our people.
You know, we've got the best people, the best team in the business with world-class capabilities built up over generations through rigorous development and challenging cross-functional assignments that really do give us the best people in the business. The way I look at it is, you know, we're gonna take those competitive advantages that are unique to us, apply them to our advantaged assets and opportunities, and that's gonna deliver leading value creation and unmatched industry-leading shareholder returns going forward. I'll just use that opportunity to say that. I also wanna say thanks to Brad and the whole team here who've been, you know, very gracious with their time, onboarding me over the last month and a half or couple of months. We've had, you know, a very kind of structured, thoughtful, rigorous handover. Thank you.
Operator
Our next question will come from Menno Hulshof with TD Cowen.
Menno Hulshof
Managing Director of Institutional Equity Research, TD Cowen
Good morning, everyone, and congrats to the both of you. I'll start with a question on the February cold snap. It sounds like in your opening comments, Brad, it sounded like things went reasonably well under the circumstances. Were there any additional learnings that came out of that beyond what was learned in 2022? Do you have any new ideas on work that could get done to mitigate downtime related to extreme cold going forward?
Brad Corson
Chairman and CEO, Imperial Oil
Yeah. Thanks, Menno, and appreciate kind of your question. I'm gonna turn it over to Cheryl in a minute. I would just reflect on, you know, this February was a challenging February from a weather standpoint. As I mentioned, you know, we learned from the 2022 incident around kind of what were some operating improvements we could put in place. We developed some additional protocols, which now we put in effect, and really leveraged them to get us through a similar period this year than what we saw in 2022, but with much better results.
You know, while I would say it was unfortunate that the net result was still lower volumes compared to last quarter or last, I'm quite proud, and I think it further demonstrated the strength of those protocols. As always, there's learnings and insights, and we're gonna continue to strive to be better in these sort of situations when they occur in the future. Maybe I'll ask Cheryl to comment a little bit on some of those, you know, insights that we gained and, you know, how we're going to learn from those in the future.
Cheryl Gomez-Smith
SVP of Upstream, Imperial Oil
Sure. Thank you, Brad. Maybe a little bit of start. The cold weather protocols we exercise extreme weather conditions. Think of this, 25 degrees Celsius, -35 degrees Celsius. What we do is reduce throughput, align with our equipment strategies, and focus on maintaining equipment integrity. February 2025 was in the Fort McMurray region one of the highest number of extreme cold days versus 2022. We applied the learnings from 2022, and the protocols worked as intended. Brad mentioned, of course, we've from a production in April very strong month with production just below our best ever, still on target to meet external guidance. In terms of what comes next, that's a great question. Going forward, we're looking at where we can build capacity and redundancy.
John Whelan
President, Imperial Oil
I mentioned during IR Investor Day some of the things that we're doing it with our hydrotransport lines. What that allows us is to further strengthen this performance going forward to quote-unquote weather the storms.
Menno Hulshof
Managing Director of Institutional Equity Research, TD Cowen
Okay, thanks for that. Oh, sorry. I think my phone cut out. I think I'm interrupting.
Operator
No, go ahead, sir. You're still open.
Menno Hulshof
Managing Director of Institutional Equity Research, TD Cowen
Okay, terrific. Yeah. Maybe, yeah, thanks for that. It's very helpful. Maybe I'll just second question is on the EBRT pilot that was touched on in the prepared remarks. Could you maybe just expand your comments on the scope of the pilot and the, I guess the more important piece is the key deliverables that you've identified that ultimately constitute success. Then how are you risking the overall chance of success of EBRT ultimately, I suppose being a catalyst for in situ expansion?
Peter Shaw
VP of Investor Relations, Imperial Oil
I'll let Cheryl comment on that again.
Cheryl Gomez-Smith
SVP of Upstream, Imperial Oil
Sure. As Brad mentioned, we're constructing a short-term small scale pilot, and this is to test the commercial potential of our Enhanced Bitumen Recovery Technology. Aspen lease in the Fort McMurray area start up in 2027, and we're gonna run the pilot for several years. There's three key areas that we really need to validate. One of them is the production uplift, the second one is around overall recovery, and then the project itself is really dependent on solvent recovery. The pilot is intended to de-risk these technologies, and this is a step that we've taken with all technology.
As highlighted before, this is a transformative technology, and it will allow us to be more globally competitive, capital efficient and highly resilient. Even though we are looking at this, we need to take the time, and this is a staged approach really to de-risk the technology. That's the time we'll be taking with the pilot going forward.
Menno Hulshof
Managing Director of Institutional Equity Research, TD Cowen
Thank you. I'll turn it back.
Operator
Thank you. That does conclude the question-and-answer session. I will now turn the conference back over to Peter Shaw, Vice President of Investor Relations for closing remarks.
Peter Shaw
VP of Investor Relations, Imperial Oil
Thank you. On behalf of the management team, I thank you for joining us this morning. If there's any further questions, please don't hesitate to reach out to anybody on the investor relations team. We'll be happy to answer your questions. With that, I'll add one more thank you to Brad for his time over the last five and a half years at Imperial, and we wish everybody on the call a great day.
Menno Hulshof
Managing Director of Institutional Equity Research, TD Cowen
Thank you.
Operator
Thank you. That does conclude today's conference. We do thank you for your participation. Have an excellent day.
