content.text:
Operator
Good day, and welcome to the Imperial Oil Q4 2024 Earnings Call. Today's conference is being recorded. At this time, I'd like to turn the conference over to Peter Shaw, Vice President of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.
Peter Shaw
VP of Investor Relations, Imperial Oil
Thank you, and good morning, everyone. Welcome to our Q4 earnings conference call. I'm joined this morning by Imperial senior management team, including Brad Corson, Chairman, President, and Chief Executive Officer. Dan Lyons, Senior Vice President, Finance and Administration. Sherri Evers, Senior Vice President of Sustainability, Commercial Development, and Product Solutions. Cheryl Gomez-Smith, Senior Vice President of the Upstream. Today's comments include reference to non-GAAP financial measures. The definitions and reconciliations of these measures can be found in our attachment six of our most recent press release and are available on our website with a link to today's conference call. Today's comments may contain forward-looking information. Any forward-looking information is not a guarantee of future performance, and actual performance and operating results can vary materially depending on a number of factors and assumptions.
Forward-looking information, the risk factors, and the assumptions are described further in detail on our Q4 earnings release that we issued earlier today. All these documents are available on SEDAR+, EDGAR, and our website, so I'd ask you to refer to those as well. Brad is going to start with some opening remarks and then hand it over to Dan, who's going to provide a financial update, and then Brad will provide an operations update. Once that is done, we will follow with the Q&A session. With that, I will turn it over to Brad for his opening remarks.
Brad Corson
Chairman, President, and CEO, Imperial Oil
Thank you, Peter, and good morning, everybody, and welcome to our Q4 and Full Year Earnings Call. I hope everyone is doing well and your New Year's off to a good start. Apologies for my scratchy voice as I recover from a cold. I'm really pleased to report another strong quarter for Imperial as we wrapped up 2024. We saw excellent operational performance across all our assets, both upstream and downstream, which largely offsets the impact of lower commodity prices on a sequential quarter-over-quarter basis. Despite the lower prices, our ability to continue to grow production and deliver strong downstream reliability resulted in a very solid end to 2024. Our upstream continues to set records, and we achieved the highest Q4 production in the past 30 years when adjusting for the XTO divestment.
We also realized the benefits of TMX Pipeline and additional egress, which resulted in much narrower and more stable differentials compared to a year ago. Our downstream business also performed very well over the quarter and contributed solid earnings with lower turnaround activity and higher utilization. We continue to benefit from the structural advantages of the Canadian market that supports stronger financial performance despite softer refinery crack spreads. Over the next few minutes, Dan and I will detail the results of a very strong quarter. Now let's review the Q4 results. Earnings for the quarter were CAD 1.225 billion with cash from operating activities of CAD 1.65 billion when excluding the impact of working capital. For the full year, earnings were CAD 4.79 billion, down slightly from the prior year.
Also worth noting that we delivered our second-highest earnings per share of CAD 9.03. These results reflect continued strong operational performance and our ability to capture value for our shareholders. In the upstream, we achieved total production of 460,000 gross oil equivalent barrels per day in the Q4. This marks the highest Q4 production over the past 30 years when adjusting for the historical volumes associated with the divested XTO assets and resulted in the highest Q4 upstream earnings in the company's history. The strong Q4 results also contributed to the highest annual upstream production in over 30 years at 433,000bbl per day, even when including the divested XTO assets.
Our strong operating performance led to a unit cash cost reduction of nearly $3 US a barrel when comparing to full year 2023. Looking ahead, we expect to continue to lower our unit cash costs based on advancing further growth and structural cost reduction initiatives. Kearl continued the year with yet another strong quarter, which resulted in us achieving the asset's highest ever annual production, exceeding 280,000bbl per day this year on a gross basis. I'm very proud of the team for achieving this production milestone, and I know they are squarely focused on carrying this momentum into 2025 and achieving even higher volumes. I'm also extremely pleased by the performance at Cold Lake. We delivered very strong performance in the Q4 with the planned turnaround activity behind us and all of the new Grand Rapids wells producing.
Our transformation of production and unit cash costs at Cold Lake is off to a great start as we leverage solvent recovery technology with impressive results. In the downstream, all our assets performed very well, and with the only planned turnaround activity in the quarter being the completion of the maintenance work at Nanticoke that we discussed on our last call. Refinery throughput averaged 411,000bbl per day, which equates to a refinery utilization in the quarter of 95% and a full-year utilization of 92%, which is at the top end of our 2024 guidance. The Q4 also saw us continue to maximize shareholder returns. We completed the accelerated NCIB in mid-December with purchases of CAD 1.475 billion in the quarter.
In addition, we paid CAD 317 million in dividends in the quarter for a total of CAD 1.2 billion in dividends for the entire year. In total, we returned CAD 3.9 billion of cash to shareholders in 2024 and CAD 16 billion over the past three years. Finally, this morning, we declared a dividend of CAD 0.72 per share payable on 1 April 2025. The CAD 0.12 per share or 20% increase is the largest nominal dividend increase in company history. This is further demonstration of our commitment to growing the dividend and returning surplus cash to shareholders. It also reflects our confidence in delivering on the guidance we communicated in December. As we move into 2025, we remain focused on our core strategy of optimizing our existing asset base to maximize shareholder value.
A strategy that has allowed us to increase our quarterly dividend per share by over 225% since 2020. With that, I'll pass things over to Dan to discuss our financial results in more detail.
Dan Lyons
SVP, Finance and Administration, Imperial Oil
Thanks, Brad. Starting with financial results for Q4. We reported net income of CAD 1.225 billion. This represents a decrease of CAD 140 million from Q4 2023, primarily as a result of lower margins in our downstream business, partially offset by higher upstream production. When comparing sequentially, Q4 net income is down slightly from Q3 2024, primarily driven by lower prices, partially offset by stronger operational performance. Now shifting our attention to each business line and looking sequentially. Upstream earnings of CAD 878 million are down CAD 149 million from Q3, primarily due to lower realizations, partially offset by higher volumes.
Downstream earnings of CAD 356 million are up CAD 151 million from Q3, mainly reflecting lower turnaround impacts. Favorable foreign exchange and inventory effects. Our chemical business generated earnings of CAD 21 million, down CAD 7 million from Q3. Moving on to cash flow. In Q4, we generated CAD 1.78 billion in cash flows from operating activities. Excluding favorable working capital effects of CAD 139 million, cash flows from operating activities for Q4 were CAD 1.65 billion, down CAD 147 million from Q3 2024. We ended the year with nearly CAD 1 billion of cash on hand.
Shifting to CapEx, capital expenditures totaled CAD 423 million in Q4, down CAD 46 million from Q4 2023. In the upstream, Q4 spending focused on sustaining and growing production at Kearl, Syncrude, and Cold Lake. In the downstream, Q4 spending mainly continued to progress our renewable diesel project at Strathcona. Full year 2024 capital expenditures totaled CAD 1.867 billion. Shifting to shareholder distributions. Consistent with our strategy to timely distribute free cash flow, we returned CAD 3.9 billion to shareholders over the course of 2024. Moving into 2025, we continue to demonstrate our long-standing philosophy to deliver a reliable and growing dividend. As Brad already noted, we declared a Q4-
I'm sorry, we declared a Q1 dividend of CAD 0.72 per share early this morning, which will be payable on 1 April. This represents an increase of 20% compared to the Q4 2024 dividend. Now I'll turn it back to Brad to discuss our operational performance.
Brad Corson
Chairman, President, and CEO, Imperial Oil
Thanks, Dan. I know you've all had a chance to look through the numbers, but I do wanna focus your attention on some of our key performance highlights. Upstream production for the quarter averaged 460,000 oil equivalent barrels per day. As I mentioned earlier, this represents the highest Q4 production in over 30 years when adjusting for the XTO divestment. Production was up 13,000bbl per day versus the Q3 and up 8,000bbl per day versus the Q4 of 2023, mainly due to higher volumes at Cold Lake. Our upstream also delivered the best full-year production in over 30 years, with 433,000 oil equivalent barrels per day. A 5% increase in total or a 14% per share increase versus full year 2023.
Now let's move on and talk specifically about Kearl's record year. Kearl's production in Q4 averaged 299,000bbl per day gross, which is up 4,000bbl per day versus Q3 and 9,000bbl per day lower versus the Q4 record previously set in 2023. As targeted, Kearl achieved over 280,000bbl per day in 2024 and set the full-year production record of 281,000bbl per day. It's also worth noting, in the last five years, we have grown Kearl production by 75,000bbl per day, which is over 35%. This marks a significant milestone in Kearl's journey to deliver record production through efficient growth initiatives and achieve unit cash costs below our previously stated target of $20 per barrel.
We've made major strides in lowering unit cash costs at Kearl over the past few years. The full-year unit cash cost of $19.67 US per barrel reflects the hard work of the entire Kearl team, not only to meet our previously set target of $20 US per barrel, but to beat it. In talking with Cheryl and the team, they continue to find new opportunities and leverage the current momentum to drive down unit cash costs even further. This is very exciting, and I look forward to sharing at our upcoming investor day some of these opportunities and how they will help to support our new target of $18 US per barrel.
As we begin 2025, Kearl is off to a very strong start and is on track to set another record with January production over 280,000bbl per day. Turning to another highlight of 2024, Cold Lake. For Q4, Cold Lake production averaged 157,000bbl per day, which is up 10,000bbl per day versus Q3 and up 18,000bbl per day versus Q4 2023. The impressive quarterly results were driven by better than expected production from the new Grand Rapids project, which has brought on lower cost barrels and starting the transformation at Cold Lake and further reducing our unit cash costs towards our stated $13 US dollar target.
The strong production resulted in unit cash costs of $14.21 US per barrel in the quarter, which is a decrease of over $1.50 US per barrel compared to the same quarter last year. On a full-year basis, our unit cash cost of $14.75 US per barrel is more than $2 US per barrel lower than last year. A major highlight this year has been our new solvent-assisted SAGD production from Grand Rapids, and it continued to impress in Q4. Last quarter, I highlighted Grand Rapids achieving an average of 15,000bbl per day and on an instantaneous basis, seeing peak rates of 22,000bbl per day.
Well, I'm pleased to be able to confirm that these volumes were maintained, resulting in an increase of 7,000bbl per day up to 22,000bbls per day for Q4. While early, our data shows clear upside on the original project funding basis of 15,000bbl per day. I continue to look forward to the first full year of Grand Rapids production in our operations in 2025 and the advancement of future solvent-assisted SAGD growth projects at Cold Lake. The next step in our transformation of the Cold Lake asset is the Leming redevelopment project. Construction continued on the facilities through the quarter, which will leverage existing infrastructure and steam capacity. Startup is expected to begin in late 2025 and average about 9,000bbl per day at peak production. Now a few comments on Syncrude.
Imperial share of Syncrude production for the quarter averaged 81,000bbl per day, which was flat versus Q3 and down 4,000bbl per day versus Q4 2023. During the quarter, Syncrude continued to utilize the interconnect pipeline to import bitumen and gas oil, driving record annual upgrader utilization rates and producing about 9,000bbl per day, our share of incremental Syncrude Sweet Premium in the quarter. As we move into 2025, we look forward to continued focus on reliability and costs at Syncrude. Now moving on to the downstream, which also had strong operations in Q4. Overall, we refined an average of 411,000bbl per day, reflecting a utilization of 95%, our highest quarter this year.
Compared to Q3, when we had turnarounds at Nanticoke and Strathcona, we processed an additional 22,000bbls per day. The strong Q4 and the successful execution of turnarounds throughout the year enabled us to achieve the top end of our 2024 full-year guidance, with throughput of 399,000bbl per day and a utilization rate of 92%. Looking ahead to 2025, we have a lighter turnaround year compared to 2024 and are on track to have the construction on the Strathcona Renewable Diesel project facilities completed in Q2, with expected first production in the middle of 2025.
Petroleum product sales in the quarter were 458,000bbl per day, which is down 29,000bbl per day versus Q3 and down 18,000bbl per day versus Q4 2023. Results year-over-year reflect some variability in discretionary sales choices and were not driven by market demand. Overall, we continue to see resilient demand in Canada with gasoline and diesel at approximately 90% and jet recovering over 100% when compared to 2019. Turning now to chemicals. Earnings in Q4 were CAD 21 million, which was down CAD 7 million versus Q3, mainly driven by lower prices, partly offset by the absence of the aromatics earnings shift in Q3, which we previously discussed.
Earnings in the quarter were up CAD 4 million versus Q4 2023 due to the absence of the prior year turnaround activity and partially offset by lower prices, and the aromatics earnings shift. In closing, this was another excellent quarter to finish off a very strong year. We achieved record volumes in our upstream, significantly reduced our upstream unit costs, and delivered high downstream utilization. As we begin 2025, I'm confident in the team at Imperial and our ability to deliver another very strong year as we continue to create significant value for shareholders by progressing on our journey to achieve the new volume and unit cash cost targets we outlined in our recent guidance. Similarly, as we look ahead in 2025, our commitment to shareholder returns is unchanged.
We have demonstrated that ongoing commitment with the accelerated completion of our NCIB in December and the announcement today of our largest nominal dividend increase ever. I'm very pleased by the operating momentum that we have carried into this new year, and I'm excited by the opportunities we have ahead of us to increase volumes, lower costs, and deliver greater free cash flow for our shareholders. Before I wrap up, I would like to recognize Sherri Evers for her many contributions and accomplishments as part of our management committee over the last four years. Her leadership of a diverse portfolio resulted in significant progress across many key areas of the business, including her instrumental role in Pathways since day one.
We wish her all the best in her new role with ExxonMobil. As always, I'd like to thank you once again for your continued interest and support. Now we'll move to the Q&A session, and I'll pass it back to Peter. Thank you.
Peter Shaw
VP of Investor Relations, Imperial Oil
Thank you, Brad. As always, we'd appreciate it if you could limit yourself to one question plus a follow-up so that we can get to as many questions as possible. With that, operator, could you please open up the lines for questions?
Operator
Thank you. If you would like to signal with questions, please press star one on your touch-tone telephone. If you're joining us today using a speakerphone, please make sure your mute function is turned off to allow your signal to reach our equipment. Again, that will be star one if you would like to signal with questions, star one. Our first question will come from the line of Manav Gupta with UBS.
Manav Gupta
Executive Director, UBS
Wanted to start by congratulating the management on another 20% dividend hike. Brad, if my memory is right, when you took over, the quarterly dividend was close to CAD 0.22, and now you have raised it to CAD 0.72 during your tenure. It does take a very strong track record of execution to achieve that. Just wanted to congratulate you on that. My first question is on refining. Your earnings are up materially quarter-over-quarter. When we look across to US refiners, the earnings are down 50% to 70% quarter-over-quarter. Help us understand what's driving the resilience of refining here. I understand you operated at a higher rate, but still, this is in stark contrast to what we are seeing for US refiners. If you can help us understand the resilience of refining here.
Brad Corson
Chairman, President, and CEO, Imperial Oil
Yeah. Thank you, Manav. First, I really appreciate your recognition of the dividend increase over the last few years. That is something our organization is quite proud of as we have continued to grow our cash flow generation abilities and obviously return that to our shareholders. We're all quite proud of that, and thanks for that recognition. In terms of the refining strength, I'd say there's a couple of drivers there. You know, first of all, as I've commented in the past, you know, the Canadian refining sector and especially our Imperial refineries are well-advantaged versus US counterparts. We have access to advantaged crudes. We continue to have strong demand in the marketplace. We have exceptional infrastructure that allows us to move our products to premium outlets.
As you also mentioned, we had really superb utilization over the quarter, which allows us to take full advantage of the market fundamentals that we see. When we put all that together, a very resilient and profitable downstream for us, and we're quite happy with that.
Manav Gupta
Executive Director, UBS
Perfect. My second is on Grand Rapids. It's clearly helping you drive production records at Cold Lake. Can you talk more about why the results of phase I actually exceeded your expectations? Any future phases as well as Leming, which can allow you to continue to grow the volumes at Cold Lake? Thank you.
Brad Corson
Chairman, President, and CEO, Imperial Oil
Yeah. Thanks for that question. We are extremely pleased with what we're seeing at Grand Rapids. Certainly higher volumes than kind of the funding basis that we previously shared with the market with an objective of 15,000bbl a day. As indicated, you know, we're seeing more in the range of 22,000bbl a day. You know, it's early days. You know, we started up Grand Rapids in terms of producing volumes back in May. You know, we have seven months or so of production runtime. I would say our reservoir engineers are very busy analyzing those results and understanding what the implications are for future phase developments at Grand Rapids. As mentioned, in the past, we have several phases in the future, and so that's very exciting.
You know, I think as time goes on, we'll be able to better describe, you know, not just the long-term productivity of Grand Rapids phase I, but what it means for broader developments at Cold Lake. Way too early to tell about Leming. You know, we're in the process of constructing it, but again, you know, it's super exciting and reaffirming, when we can start up a production, you know, project like Grand Rapids, which as you recall, we accelerated by about a year. We, you know, accelerated it, and now we're seeing more production and all that adds a lot of value. You know, I think just an exciting signal of what's ahead for the future.
Manav Gupta
Executive Director, UBS
Thank you.
Operator
The next question will come from Dennis Fong with CIBC.
Dennis Fong
Equity Research Analyst, CIBC
Hi, good morning, and thanks for taking my questions. I guess the first one here is, I guess congratulations on another strong quarter at Kearl. I was actually hoping you could kind of dive in a little bit more into initiatives that you are currently undergoing that are helping kind of maintain, again, these high levels of performance. Namely kind of focusing on maybe a little bit around the autonomous fleet as well as some of the technological advancements that you are applying to production.
Brad Corson
Chairman, President, and CEO, Imperial Oil
It's a great question, Dennis. As you know, I'm super proud of what the team's been able to achieve at Kearl. It's just been kind of a steady, you know, steady result of record after record after record. As you know from the guidance we set out in December, we are anticipating further production records, further reduction in unit cash costs. The net result of that is continued, you know, growth in cash generation. Cheryl is sitting right next to me here, and you know, she's got her hand on the wheel for Kearl. I'm gonna let her make a couple comments about, you know, specific to some of those growth initiatives.
Cheryl Gomez-Smith
SVP, Upstream, Imperial Oil
Great. Thank you, Brad. As Brad mentioned, we're continuing to transform our mining business. I think it's important to start with the exceptional progress that we made in 2024 and how we're rapidly improving competitiveness. In that space, I'll highlight a few things. We're gonna continue on our journey with reliability and maintenance improvements. The second part is around mine fleet productivity gains, and this gets to your question specifically about our AHS trucks. I'm pleased to report that we've seen anywhere from 8% to 10% increase in productivity resulting from the automated trucks. We're gonna continue with debottlenecking and optimization, including digital initiatives, and we've got a full slate of digital that we're leveraging across the board, both within the plant as well as the mine.
Finally, I'll anchor it in. We're really building a continuous improvement culture. It's looking for those next opportunities across all that slate. Plenty of opportunities as we look forward, but I think the most important is building on that foundation of 2024.
Brad Corson
Chairman, President, and CEO, Imperial Oil
Thanks for that, Cheryl. Cheryl mentioned this continuous improvement mindset, and I have to brag a little bit on one example of that is around our turnaround duration. You'll recall how just a few years ago, we were doing two turnarounds a year, each one about 35 days in duration, so about 70 days total. We took a decision to reduce from two turnarounds a year to one turnaround a year, extend that interval between turnarounds from 12 months to 24 months. That took us from 70 days to about 35 days. Since then, the team continues to look for ways to improve on the efficiency of those turnarounds. This last year, they completed the single turnaround in less than 20 days.
We've gone from 70 days a year to 20 days a year, and we're taking some steps in this year's turnaround to equip ourselves to potentially extend the interval even further and reduce that annual, turnaround impact to something even less than what we've seen historically. Just another great example of how the team, you know, continues to capture benefits, but doesn't stop there, looks for what's next. I think that's a good example.
Dennis Fong
Equity Research Analyst, CIBC
Appreciate that underlying context and just kind of the holistic approach that you're taking to development. My second question, and if you'll indulge me, taking it in a slightly different direction. You've obviously done a great job executing on projects that grow and develop existing assets within your portfolio. Can you remind me a little bit on the priorities the company has or focuses on when you're allocating capital, whether it be growth, M&A, and/or shareholder returns? Specifically to you, Brad, obviously you have a prior position to this one, historical experience with evaluating assets both within your portfolio and outside of the company, how you kind of rank and order and even look or evaluate how you examine your existing portfolio versus what or how you can make it better. Thanks.
Brad Corson
Chairman, President, and CEO, Imperial Oil
Yeah. Thanks for that question. I'll offer a few comments, and Dan may want to jump in as well. I mean, fundamentally on our capital allocation strategy, it is underpinned by this long-standing approach, commitment, principle that we are going to return surplus cash to our shareholders. That starts with this reliable and growing dividend, you know, and as you saw today, we've actioned that with another very material dividend increase. We then look at you know, other opportunities to efficiently return surplus cash to shareholders. Our NCIB has been our go-to for many years.
Then where we've had additional capacity beyond that, we've looked to exercise an SIB, and we've done a few of those in our history and maintain the aperture for that in the future. You know, that's kind of the basic building blocks of our capital allocation. I guess I should mention debt as well. You know, we're at a level of debt that we're very comfortable with, so we don't see, you know, really a priority to pay down debt at this point. We're at a very low level of debt leverage. So we're quite comfortable with that. Then the question on M&A opportunities, you know, really comes to looking at potential opportunities outside our portfolio versus what we already have within our portfolio.
We're in, I think, the really unique position of having a deep inventory of really high-quality investment opportunities. You know, we're allocating capital for those as they relate to the existing assets. You know, you hear us talk about what we're doing at Kearl, at Cold Lake, what we're doing at Strathcona. Looking to the future, you know, we're quite excited by the potential of the Aspen project. We're actively progressing a pilot project that will allow us to fully validate and commercialize the EBRT solvent technology, which we believe, you know, will significantly unlock value for Aspen relative to other solvent technologies. That's a very material investment for us, material production growth opportunity. As we look at other M&A opportunities, we're comparing those to things like Aspen.
Strategically, to pursue an acquisition, it needs to compete with what's already in our portfolio. It needs to have unique synergies and be really consistent with our longer-term strategies. That aperture is open. We have an internal team of folks that are regularly evaluating opportunities. But up till now, you know, we haven't seen anything that we believe is more value accretive than the projects within our portfolio like Aspen. We don't need to make an acquisition, but we're looking for something if it makes sense. That's how I would characterize that. Dan, anything else on capital allocation?
Dan Lyons
SVP, Finance and Administration, Imperial Oil
No, I think you covered it well, Brad. You know, just to maybe summarize, the reliable and growing dividend is sort of the first place, the first stop for our free cash flow. Then we go to sustaining capital, and then we look at high return growth projects, which would include, as Brad said, potential M&A. You know, it's a high bar given our return expectations in our internal portfolio. Then since we're happy with our debt level, after that, it's return of the surplus cash to shareholders. That's set in a timely way. We're no change to that. It's been our consistent posture for quite a while.
Dennis Fong
Equity Research Analyst, CIBC
Great. Really appreciate the context from both of you. I'll turn it back. Thank you.
Operator
The next question will come from Greg Pardy with RBC.
Greg Pardy
Analyst, RBC
Yeah, thanks. Good morning. Thanks for the rundown, Brad, and maybe just first off, you know, just all the very best to Cheryl going to XOM. Wanted to ask you really on two fronts. One is tactical, a little bit more around Cold Lake. Probably the bigger one is how are you thinking about the, you know, the tariff threat that you've got going on? I'm sure you know you've had time to analyze that, and then there's the relationship with ExxonMobil. How well equipped are you to withstand something like that? Secondly is as it relates to shareholder returns, you know, is it really just essentially driven by cash balances?
In other words, if we did see tariffs and cash balances still ticked up to levels where you could repurchase stock, how would you sort of think about those? I know, very hypothetical, but obviously, you know, just a huge issue obviously overhang Canada right now.
Brad Corson
Chairman, President, and CEO, Imperial Oil
All right. Thanks. Thanks for that, Greg. Yeah, obviously a lot of interest and discussion over tariffs, you know, really across all sectors, but especially energy. You know, as I've talked in the past, US and Canada are really strong energy partners and benefit from each other. The US heavily dependent on Canada's heavy crude. We don't know what's gonna happen with tariffs. You know, I don't have any unique insight, but I, along with many others, have spent a lot of time educating on both sides of the border around kind of the unique and integral energy system that exists and how that is mutually beneficial to both countries.
You know, I'm hopeful that as we move forward, diplomacy will prevail and, you know, we will end up with no tariffs, no restrictions on energy flow. I believe that's a win-win scenario. Anything else, any tariffs, will result in negative impacts, you know, broadly to the economy and customers. Let's hope we avoid those. I can't control that. What we're focused on is what can we control. What we control is ensuring that we have you know, the lowest cost of supply. We have options for where we place our crude and products in the market. We're trying to do that at the lowest possible cost, and I believe that gives us unique resilience. You know, we obviously produce a heavy crude.
We also are acquiring light crudes to meet our refinery runs. You know, some of those, even as we see, if heavy crudes are impacted negatively with value, we would expect to see some offset of that with the light crudes that we're running in our refinery. The strength of integration, I think, makes us much more resilient than others. You know, 1 February appears to be a big day for tariffs. You know, we'll be watching that closely. I am confident that you know, we will continue to be you know, profitable. We'll continue to generate material cash flow and be in a position to return that to our shareholders. That clearly underpinned our decision to raise the dividend today.
Dan, anything you wanna talk about with respect to shareholder returns or anything like that?
Dan Lyons
SVP, Finance and Administration, Imperial Oil
Yeah, Greg, you know, you had kind of asked if, you know, returns to shareholders and buybacks in particular would be driven primarily by cash balances or other factors, like the tariffs. I would say it's gonna be primarily by cash balances. You know, especially given our low breakevens, our ability to generate, you know, cash going forward through a range of environments, our low debt level. You know, we don't need to have a huge amount of cash to, sort of, you know, protect us going forward. However, of course, we'll take into account the environment, whatever is happening at the time as we make those decisions. Generally speaking, our philosophy has been consistent. It's timely return of surplus cash to shareholders.
Greg Pardy
Analyst, RBC
Okay. Yeah, very, very logical. Brad, I wanted to come back to your, you know, your thinking just around acquisitions versus organic. You know, I've mentioned before, every company seems to have significant growth initiatives underway right now. When you kind of weigh acquisitions where there may already be an egress solution in place versus your organic growth initiatives, where there potentially could be some limitations on pipe capacity and so forth, is that kind of dialed into your thinking when you go through that LP model?
Brad Corson
Chairman, President, and CEO, Imperial Oil
Yeah, certainly, we would look at all aspects of that. You know, we'd look at what's the cost competitiveness of an opportunity? What's the long-term running room of an opportunity? What are any unique egress considerations? Are there unique tax pool considerations? What's the carbon intensity? So we'll take all those things into account. You know, back to my earlier comment, at least up until this point, when we look at the value we see of an Aspen development, it wins relative to anything else we would see when we look at all those factors together.
Greg Pardy
Analyst, RBC
Perfect. Thanks very much.
Brad Corson
Chairman, President, and CEO, Imperial Oil
Thanks, Greg.
Operator
We have a question from Menno Hulshof with TD Securities.
Menno Hulshof
Managing Director, Institutional Equity Research, TD Securities
Thanks, and good morning, everyone. I'll start with a question on TMX. Can we just get an update on the status of toll negotiations? Last I heard, and it's been a while, but I believe the guide was from some of your peers, was that it could be a mid-year event. With all the uncertainties, including tariffs, is it fair to assume that mid-year is too optimistic at this stage? Thank you.
Brad Corson
Chairman, President, and CEO, Imperial Oil
Yeah, Menno, thanks for that question. I don't have a very specific update on that. You know, our teams are certainly directly engaged on it. I don't have a very specific outlook on what's a refresh timing. I would say obviously that, you know, more broadly speaking, we've been very pleased with the operation, the start of the operation of TMX, and we are shipping on it on a regular basis. That's really all I'm in a position to comment on at this point.
Menno Hulshof
Managing Director, Institutional Equity Research, TD Securities
Got it. Thanks, Brad, for that. Maybe the second question would be on Strathcona. Already in the press release you reiterated that you're still tracking to a mid-year startup, but can we maybe just get a bit more detail in terms of what still needs to happen to get that project across the line? When you think about sort of cash flow positivity, is it possible that we see that in the second half of 2025, or is that more likely a 2026 event?
Brad Corson
Chairman, President, and CEO, Imperial Oil
Yeah. Thanks for the question. I mean, we're certainly excited by this project. It's, you know, we view it as quite strategic for us to expand our slate of product offerings to the market. It's a really important opportunity for us to help decarbonize the industry. So we view it as very positive. As you'll recall, there's multiple components to the project. You know, at the core of the project is the manufacturing facility that we're building at Strathcona Refinery. And that construction is well advanced. Modules have been delivered. We're in the process of hooking them up, and we expect to complete that construction in Q2, which would then position us to start production, you know, somewhere a lot around mid-year.
Now, also two other really key integral components is, first of all, the vegetable or agricultural oil supply stream. We have been in the process of negotiating supply arrangements and, you know, we have sufficient supply established for us to be able to start this unit up. We're looking at, you know, longer term relationships as well. That work continues, ready to start up. The third really important component is the supply of hydrogen. That work is underway by Air Products, and also, you know, working to be in a position to supply us with, you know, initial supplies beginning in this Q2, mid-year timing.
When we start up, I would expect we'll be at some reduced rates as part of, you know, a typical startup. Then over time, as we look at, you know, how to optimize each of those components with market conditions, you know, that'll determine how quickly we ramp up, what's the ultimate product volumes. Really just like any other product in our refinery, you know, that we're constantly optimizing over time, based on the cost and availability of feedstocks coupled with market conditions and demand for the product. We feel really good about being able to start up mid-year. In terms of positive cash flow, yeah, we view this as a very profitable undertaking for us, and we would expect to see positive cash flow in the second half of this year.
Operator
Moving on to Neil Mehta with Goldman Sachs.
Neil Mehta
Managing Director, Goldman Sachs
Thanks so much, Brad and team. I just wanted to spend some time on upstream cash costs, where I know you guys are targeting CAD 18 at Kearl and CAD 13 at Cold Lake. Where are you in that journey? What's the next step, and what did this quarter tell you about your ability to ultimately get there?
Brad Corson
Chairman, President, and CEO, Imperial Oil
Yeah, thanks for the question. I mean, we're well on the journey, you know? We're obviously below CAD 20 at Kearl now. We're in the CAD 14 range at Cold Lake, and so well on our way. Maybe I'll ask Cheryl just to make a couple of comments about some of the near term initiatives that we have underway. You know, as we laid out that guidance back in December, we feel quite confident in being able to achieve that.
Cheryl Gomez-Smith
SVP, Upstream, Imperial Oil
Sure. Thanks, Brad. Let me add a little bit more about Kearl starting with, which is, when we think about what's gonna enable us to get to that $18 unit cash goal, it's really about leveraging the scale that we have, as well as continued focus on reliability and optimization. As we have that incremental production, we're gonna be leveraging basically our fixed cost structure at Kearl, and that's a very powerful lever in terms of lowering our unit costs. You heard me mention before, it's that continued focus on reliability, maintenance optimization, plus deployment of digital solutions. That in itself will get us to improve productivity as well as lower absolute costs. If I think about the Cold Lake side, that too is gonna be leveraging our scale.
As we grow our production mix to these higher volumes, that's gonna leverage that fixed cost base, but we're also introducing lower cost barrels into the mix. As we and Brad mentioned about the progress, the early insights that we're getting from Grand Rapids as a SAGD, as we continue this year with Leming, which are lower cost infills. We're both growing and transforming the volumes at Cold Lake. It's both a numerator and a denominator opportunity at both Cold Lake as well as Kearl.
Neil Mehta
Managing Director, Goldman Sachs
Well, that's the follow-up. It's just the Kearl you talked about 280, 290 this year with the goal of getting to +300. I guess the question is, how plus is plus, you know? Just your perspective on, in a capital efficient way, how big could Kearl be, in the context of the budget that you laid out?
Brad Corson
Chairman, President, and CEO, Imperial Oil
Yeah, thanks. I'll try to answer that. You know, I think it's too early to tell how big plus could be. The reason we shared that guidance is we do see the potential for future volumes above 300. You know, how much above 300 will be determined by our ability to continue to unlock, you know, cost-efficient barrels as we go forward. You know, we've been on this journey, you know, for five years now, if not longer, but especially the last five years, you know, where we were at around 200, 205 back in 2019. We've continued to take, you know, very thoughtful, very capital efficient steps to enable us to grow that.
As announced, you know, we set a record last year. We set another record this year, now at 281,000. We see, you know, an increasing number of days that are above 300,000 for individual days, and in some cases, weeks and months. Now, you know, what the team's focused on is how can they string together more of those days, and of course, be able to offset any planned downtime like a turnaround. We see the potential for something above 300, but until we knock down barriers to get us from 280 to 290 and heading towards 300, I don't know that we fully realize what that potential is. We're gonna only pursue it, you know, if it's capital efficient.
We've got a great base there, you know, with material fixed costs. Generally, if we can add additional barrels, they're gonna come at a lower variable cost to us, and that adds value to the cash flow for the asset. More work to come there, but you know, I hope as you've seen us demonstrate over the last couple of years, we're laser focused on it.
Neil Mehta
Managing Director, Goldman Sachs
Thank you, Brad.
Operator
The next question will come from Doug Leggate with Wolfe Research.
Doug Leggate
Managing Director and Senior Research Analyst, Wolfe Research
Hey, good morning, everybody. Thanks for taking my questions. Hey, Brad, happy New Year. So I've got two break-even questions, if I may. They both may be Dan's bailiwick, but I'd love your perspective on it. First of all, someone, I think it was Manav or Greg touched on the dividend earlier. 20% is another sizable bump, obviously. What I'm curious about is where do you see your break-even today with the CapEx on the growth of whether it's today or whether it's projected on where you see the growth going, how does your break-even evolve? Because that headroom for dividend growth remains a potent advantage for you guys relative to your peers.
My follow-up is also kind of a break-even question related to the balance sheet. You guys have got a stellar, one of the best, if not the best balance sheet in the industry and have done for a long time. When we think about SIB, we tend to think about the question earlier about cash balances. We don't really think about, well, yeah, but you've also got this stellar balance sheet. I'm wondering if you could give us an idea, where would you be comfortable with your balance sheet moving to over time? I guess if I could circle back on the dividend question, where would you be comfortable with the dividend break even moving to over time? I appreciate the chance to ask the question.
Brad Corson
Chairman, President, and CEO, Imperial Oil
Yeah. Thanks, Doug. Happy New Year. I'll let Dan take those questions. But first, I would just emphasize the work we have done to grow volume, to lower unit cost continues to allow us to improve our break even. You know, what we're doing with the dividend is integral to that strategy. I believe we've said our break even, including dividend, is about $35 a barrel, but I'll let Dan kind of walk you through that.
Dan Lyons
SVP, Finance and Administration, Imperial Oil
Yeah. Thanks, Brad. Hey, Doug. Yeah. You know, we had this last guidance call, I guess we had in December, which included of course our you know most current outlooks on volumes and capital and everything. We said our cash breakeven was you know for WTI US dollars less than $25, and for you know with dividends and sustaining capital less than $35. So those are great numbers, obviously. As Brad pointed out, we continue to you know. Our goal is to work that down through volume growth and unit cash cost reductions, which give you headroom you know for dividend increases and other things and keeping the breakeven tight. You know, I would say we like the low breakevens, but we're not wedded to them.
You know, those are pretty low and, you know, that wouldn't, you know, it wouldn't stop us from growing the dividend if we were above some, you know, if our breakeven went up a little bit. I mean, that's a good reason for the breakeven to go up, is you've increased your dividend. A bad reason would be, you know, higher unit costs and things like that. I can't give you detailed numbers except to say, we're gonna keep working on the breakeven side with our volumes and unit cash costs. On the dividend side, you know, what we do is we look out over a future period, we put some conservative assumptions on that, and we say, "Okay.
What kind of dividend increase could we sustain?" That's kind of our model, and that's what led to this, you know, 20% dividend increase this year and last year, in fact. We see, you know, with our outlooks, even at conservative, you know, estimates, room to continue to grow our dividend in a robust fashion. We'll always be careful and make sure it's sustainable. That's probably not getting to the detail, but hopefully that gives you some more color on our thinking.
Doug Leggate
Managing Director and Senior Research Analyst, Wolfe Research
It does. Dan, what about the balance sheet in terms of the SIB? Because obviously you've got a lot of headroom if you did wanna take advantage of that.
Dan Lyons
SVP, Finance and Administration, Imperial Oil
I feel like we answered this question just recently, maybe the prior earnings call. I'm not sure. Yeah, look, is it possible we could borrow to buy back shares? It certainly is. It hasn't been our practice. We've said we're happy with our debt level, about CAD 4 billion. You know, we're kind of returning 100% of free cash flow beyond that. You know, certainly we would be willing to leverage our balance sheet for attractive investment opportunities, M&A things that make sense for us. We're creative, we met our criteria. It certainly remains a possibility for buybacks. You know, that's not what we've historically done. Maybe I'll just leave it at that.
Doug Leggate
Managing Director and Senior Research Analyst, Wolfe Research
Yeah. Dan, I don't want everyone listening to think I'm a complete lunatic, so let me just clarify the question, then I'll let you guys go. Sorry for this. I guess the way I think about it is you can borrow at a very, very low cost to fund your projects, your growth at Kearl, and the tremendous free cash flow you have is available for the SIB. I think about it more as leveraging for, as a sort of project finance as opposed to. At the end of the day, cash is cash.
Dan Lyons
SVP, Finance and Administration, Imperial Oil
Good point.
Doug Leggate
Managing Director and Senior Research Analyst, Wolfe Research
I get it. Thank you so much, guys, for the answers, and I appreciate the time.
Dan Lyons
SVP, Finance and Administration, Imperial Oil
We don't think you're a lunatic, Doug.
Operator
The next question will come from Patrick O'Rourke with ATB Capital Markets.
Patrick O'Rourke
Managing Director, Institutional Equity Research, ATB Capital Markets
Good morning, guys. Congratulations on the dividend increase and very comprehensive rundown so far. I'll just ask a couple of quick questions here. I guess, you know, you talked about sort of the final steps with getting the renewable diesel facility on. There's a little bit of noise in the renewable and the LCFS market here with, you know, I think there's an anti-dumping lawsuit that's been launched. Can you maybe walk us through some of the puts and takes around that market? You've talked about, you know, sort of transportation advantage offtake for Imperial here out of the facility and how you're viewing the market and the risks right now.
Brad Corson
Chairman, President, and CEO, Imperial Oil
Yeah. Thanks for the question, Patrick. I've talked about this a little bit in the past, you know. There are certainly other examples of renewable diesel projects, you know, on both sides of the border that are struggling. Our project is very unique and very different and, you know, should not be characterized the same as these other challenged projects. We have multiple attributes that are quite favorable to our economic proposition, starting with the fact that, you know, we are building this renewable diesel facility within our existing Strathcona facility, which gives us tremendous economies of scale, unique aspects to utilities, to rail facilities, all those sorts of things that allow it to be more efficient than a standalone facility somewhere else. So that's a big plus for us.
Secondly, you know, we are building it to process agricultural crops, and oils from them that are readily available in close proximity. The transportation costs for those oils is quite affordable, quite efficient. We're also leveraging a proprietary catalyst from ExxonMobil that will allow us to produce a premium product relative to its utility over a wide range of operating conditions, especially cold weather. That allows it to be a 100% drop in fuel for regular diesel. Does not have to be blended as much. It can be, but doesn't have to be. It can be used year-round versus just seasonally. All those things are advantaged.
On top of that, what also underpins the economics is we already have in our product offering a base level demand for renewable fuels to blend. Today we purchase those on the market. In the future, we'll now be producing them ourselves, and more cost efficiently than buying from somebody else. That enhances the economics. Certainly a lot of, you know, questions about what's the future of the carbon market. You know, I would just offer there that we plan to sell this product into multiple provincial markets, which many of them have their own stated carbon policies and requirements for low carbon fuel. You know, when I put all that together, we continue to believe we have a differentiated offering here relative to others. I hope that helps clarify that.
Patrick O'Rourke
Managing Director, Institutional Equity Research, ATB Capital Markets
Yeah, no, that's terrific and very comprehensive. Just sort of secondly, this is sort of on the political front here, but with, you know, sort of a prorogation in parliament and potentially a bit of shift in sentiment towards carbon here, both, you know, from both sides of the political spectrum. I'm wondering if you can provide an update on the Pathways Alliance here. I know that there were some of the sort of critical long lead time items that need to be ordered in very short order and sort of what the plan is with respect to that as we head towards the end of the year.
Brad Corson
Chairman, President, and CEO, Imperial Oil
Yeah. Patrick, that's a great question. An important opportunity for me to reemphasize that, you know, the six companies that have formed together, the Pathways Alliance, and have been working together for multiple years, continue to see the importance and the value of decarbonizing our industry. You know, that's what brought us together. Irrespective of, you know, political parties, we believe that's important. You know, we in Canada, I think, are blessed with a tremendous endowment of resources, third-largest oil reserves in the world, and that puts us in a tremendous position to support, you know, energy availability globally. To be competitive and sustainable long term, our view is we need to be cost competitive and we need to be carbon competitive.
To be carbon competitive over the long term, we need to continue to look to decarbonize. Our discussions with the governments, federal and provincial, continue as we look to establish all the necessary fiscal support and regulatory policy support so that we can progress an investment. We still have work to do there. You know, we're not at the point yet of committing to the pipe, which is kind of the first critical step. As you point out, you know, there is some urgency around that, based on our original objective of a 2030 startup. As time goes on, you know, it becomes increasingly difficult to meet that startup timing.
We continue the work and, you know, we continue the engineering work, we continue the permitting work, we continue the environmental studies, we continue the indigenous collaboration, all with an objective of moving this project forward, you know, as timely as we can because we think it's important. More to come. You know, hopefully we'll get further clarity from the governments on, you know, these open items and we can move forward.
Patrick O'Rourke
Managing Director, Institutional Equity Research, ATB Capital Markets
Thank you.
Operator
Thank you. That does conclude the Q&A session. I'll now hand it back over to Peter Shaw for any additional or closing remarks.
Peter Shaw
VP of Investor Relations, Imperial Oil
Thank you, everybody, and on behalf of the management team, we want to thank you for joining our call today. If you have any further questions, please don't hesitate to reach out to anybody on the IR team, and we'd be happy to answer your questions. With that, thank you very much and have a great day and great weekend.
Operator
Thank you. That does conclude today's conference. We do thank you for your participation and have an excellent day.

content.text:
Operator
Good day, and Welcome to the Imperial Oil Q2 2024 Earnings Call. Today's conference is being recorded. At this time, I would like to turn the conference over to Peter Shaw, Vice President of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.
Peter Shaw
VP and Investor Relations, Imperial Oil
Morning, everyone. Welcome to our Q2 Earnings Conference Call. I'm joined this morning by Imperial's senior management team, including Brad Corson, Chairman, President, and CEO. Dan Lyons, Senior Vice President, Finance and Administration. Sherri Evers, Senior Vice President of Sustainability, Commercial Development, and Product Solutions, and Cheryl Gomez-Smith, Senior Vice President of the Upstream. Today's comments include reference to non-GAAP financial measures. The definitions and reconciliations of these measures can be found in attachment six of our most recent press release and are available on our website with a link to today's conference call. Today's comments may also contain forward-looking information. Any forward-looking information is not a guarantee of future performance and actual performance, and operating results can vary materially depending on a number of factors and assumptions.
Forward-looking information, the risk factors, and assumptions are described in further detail in our Q2 earnings release that we issued this morning, as well as our most recent Form 10-K. All these documents are available on SEDAR+, EDGAR, and our website. I would ask that you refer to those. Brad is gonna start with some opening remarks and then hand it over to Dan, who is going to provide a financial update, and then Brad will provide operations update. Once that is done, we will follow with the Q&A session. With that, I will turn it over to Brad for his opening remarks.
Brad Corson
Chairman, President, and CEO, Imperial Oil
Thank you, Peter. Good morning, everybody, and welcome to our Q2 earnings call. I hope everyone is doing well. I wanted to start today's call by taking a moment to talk about the serious wildfire situation that has occurred across Western Canada over the past few weeks. We are deeply thankful for the courageous work of the emergency services as they battle the fires in very difficult conditions to keep our community safe. Our thoughts are with the community of Jasper and others who have been tragically impacted by the destruction of the devastating fires and now as the communities work to rebuild. There have been large fires in the Fort McMurray region near our Kearl operations and to a lesser extent, around Cold Lake.
The teams at our operations have been working closely with local and provincial agencies to ensure we're taking necessary precautions to protect our people and our assets. Fortunately, to date, there have been no impacts to our production, and the situation has improved over the past few days. Of course, it's a situation that we will continue to closely monitor and take appropriate actions. Now, turning to our performance over the quarter. Our upstream saw record production coupled with stronger price realizations due to the combined benefit of strengthening WTI prices and the tightening of WCS crude differential. We were pleased to see the successful startup of TMX in May, bringing additional egress capacity for Western Canadian crudes, which has resulted in structural tightening of the differential, reduced price volatility, and a net benefit to Imperial.
Our downstream business also performed well over the quarter and contributed very solid earnings despite significant turnaround activity and some softening of refinery crack spreads. The downstream continues to realize the structural benefits of the Canadian market, including advantaged feedstocks and import parity pricing. Now let's review the Q2 results. I'm very pleased to report a strong Q2, with earnings per share up over 80% year-over-year. These results were underpinned by strong operations that included the safe and successful execution of several major planned turnaround activities across our integrated portfolio. While we still have some scheduled turnaround work ahead, we're well positioned for a strong second half of the year.
Earnings for the quarter were CAD 1.133 billion, with cash from operating activities of CAD 1.508 billion when excluding the impact of working capital. I'm very pleased by the strong financial results we achieved, especially from a quarter which included significant planned turnarounds both in the upstream and downstream. In the upstream, we achieved total production of 404,000 gross oil equivalent barrels per day in Q2. This marks the highest ever Q2 production over the past 30 years when adjusting for the sale of XTO in 2022. The results were underpinned by strong and reliable operations across all of our assets and successful turnaround execution at Kearl and Syncrude. Kearl had another fantastic quarter and matched the asset's record for highest Q2 production.
This result contributed to achieving the highest first half production in the asset's history. You may recall, this follows a record second half in 2023. Cold Lake also saw a strong Q2, including first production from our Grand Rapids Phase 1 project, the industry's first solvent assisted SAGD operation, which we will discuss in more detail shortly. In the downstream, we continue to see strong operating performance as well. Refinery throughput averaged 387,000 barrels per day, which equates to a refinery utilization in the quarter of 89% and includes the successful month-long turnarounds at both Sarnia and Strathcona. Overall, we feel very positive about the strong first half of the year and are well-positioned to meet our annual guidance. We continue to deliver significant value to our shareholders through our reliable and growing dividend and share repurchase programs.
Consistent with our commitment to return surplus cash to shareholders, we announced this morning our plans to accelerate repurchases under the normal course issuer bid with a target to complete the program prior to the end of this year. With that, I'll pass things over to Dan to discuss our financial results in more detail.
Dan Lyons

Thanks, Brad. On top of that what is also unique versus what you see in the US is the regulatory environment that we have here, the Clean Fuel Regulations, the economic support that that provides. Also, in British Columbia, there's some additional regulatory incentives. All of those things together put us in a different but much better place than what you might see in the US. Again, we feel quite good about it.
Adam Wijaya
Equity Research Associate, Goldman Sachs
Got it. That's super helpful. Maybe just shifting gears over to chemicals for a moment and the margin environment. What are you seeing in your own system from a demand standpoint, specifically on margins? How do you think about the supply-demand landscape evolving over the next, call it, couple of years with some global supply as expected? Thank you.
Brad Corson
Chairman, President, and CEO, Imperial Oil
Yeah, we're seeing obviously some strong performance out of our chemicals business. Generally flat with what we saw a year ago, but still quite material to us. We've seen continued strength in demand, some strengthening of polyethylene realizations, which have been at somewhat depressed levels for a while driven by global supply demand fundamentals.
We are seeing that strengthening as we come out of this cycle. But probably equally importantly are the strategic advantages we have of our chemicals business, recognizing it's integral to our Sarnia refinery, which may be somewhat analogous to what I just talked about with renewable diesel at Strathcona. The chemical plant is integral.
We benefit from economies of scale with Sarnia access to off gas from the refinery. We have available ethylene supply to us in the region, and we produce a premium product with a unique customer base in close proximity. We don't have significant transportation logistics to get to our customers. Again, all that leads to a strong chemicals business for us, which has demonstrated its resilience over the full cycle that we see globally.
Adam Wijaya
Equity Research Associate, Goldman Sachs
Got it. Thanks so much.
Operator
Your next question comes from the line of Doug Leggate with Wolfe Research.
Doug Leggate
Managing Director and Senior Research Analyst, Wolfe Research
Hey, good morning, guys. Thanks for having me on. How are you doing, Brad?
Brad Corson
Chairman, President, and CEO, Imperial Oil
I'm doing well, Doug. Welcome back.
Doug Leggate
Managing Director and Senior Research Analyst, Wolfe Research
Thank you. It's, I'd love to say that garden leave is a thing. It turns out it's a nightmare, but we'll talk about some other time. Anyway, two quick questions, if I may. I wanted to ask you about. I know Kearl has been kinda beaten to death for a while, but you guys have been knocking out of the park for several years now. I wanna understand what the maintenance scheduling, what role that plays in the potential, I don't wanna call it debottlenecking, but the ability to enhance the long-term production capacity.
We've seen obviously your one of your competitors obviously change their maintenance scheduling to instead of once every year, once every couple of years. What have you guys been doing there, and what role is that playing in changing the production capacity? My follow-up is a quick one for Dan. I just wonder, with everything that's going on today, coming out of maintenance, Dan, where would you say your dividend breakeven is today? Those are my two questions for you guys.
Brad Corson
Chairman, President, and CEO, Imperial Oil
All right. Thanks. Thanks, Doug. I'm inferring that your question around, turnarounds is mainly applicable to Kearl.
Doug Leggate
Managing Director and Senior Research Analyst, Wolfe Research
Yes.
Brad Corson
Chairman, President, and CEO, Imperial Oil
For Kearl, this has been a significant focus of ours, and I think an area that we are a leader in this space. If you go back to 2021 at Kearl and prior to that, we were typically having two turnarounds per year, which would be one on each train, and they were roughly an average of 35 days each, so about 70 days of turnaround activities. Subsequent to that, in the 2021–2022-time frame, we were able to demonstrate to ourselves that we could shift from two turnarounds a year to one turnaround a year. That obviously allowed us to reduce our volume impacts of turnarounds in half and also significantly reduce our cost structure at Kearl.
That, now that we have a few years of runtime on that, has proven very successful for us. Every time we do one of those turnarounds on extended interval, it further validates the decision we took and our ability to maintain the full integrity, reliability of the system, but with less downtime. We further now have employed more technology more opportunities to take that one turnaround per year and now shorten it to less than 20 days. That's what I was referring to in my earlier comments about we've now achieved essentially a 19-day turnaround, which is our only turnaround for the year. You compare that to a few years ago when we had 70 days per year. 70 to 19.
Dan Lyons
SVP, Finance and Administration, and Controller, Imperial Oil
Right.
Brad Corson
Chairman, President, and CEO, Imperial Oil
Huge improvement in our overall production capability, huge improvement in our cost structure. I would just say we're not done yet. The team is actively working on further opportunities to reduce the duration of our turnarounds. I'm quite encouraged by that. All that, of course, then translates to more production from Kearl. It's part of our roadmap that's got us to 280 for this year. We expect to 300 in future years. It's allowing us to reduce our cost structure from the high 20s US per barrel down to a target of $20 this year. We believe there's an opportunity to go even lower than $20. Huge value at Kearl.
I think that's a great lead into Dan to talk about what does that mean about breakeven, dividends, and all that thing.
Dan Lyons
SVP, Finance and Administration, and Controller, Imperial Oil
Yeah. Doug, I heard you say dividend. What was your specific question about the dividend?
Doug Leggate
Managing Director and Senior Research Analyst, Wolfe Research
Yeah. Basically, I don't know if you got a chance to look at our reinstatement materials, but there's extraordinary correlation or market recognition of value with long-term sustainable dividend growth on a per share basis. You guys, you've led, I don't wanna make the pitch here, but you've led the whole industry, not just your Canadian peers, but the global majors. However, the big difference is you've still got a relatively low yield, and we think a lot of firepower to sustain that dividend growth relative to peers that maybe don't have, right?
What I'm trying to figure out is, where do you see your dividend breakeven today so that we can get a handle on what the sustainable growth capacity continues to be for Imperial? Because ultimately, that's what we think drives your share price. I hope that's a clear enough articulation of the question.
Dan Lyons
SVP, Finance and Administration, and Controller, Imperial Oil
Yeah, no, I'll try to get it clear. As we've said before, our breakeven with sustaining capital and dividends, for our last investor day, about $35 WTI. As you well stated our philosophy is to have reliable and growing dividend. Both of those are important. We want to continue to grow it strongly as we have in the past. When I got here, I think the dividend was CAD 0.16 a share, now it's CAD 0.60. We've had some strong growth. It's important that that growth be sustainable. We look at the breakeven closely. We look at various scenarios.
I think and certainly we believe we have room for continued strong growth. It goes to what really Brad was saying. How do we do that? Well, it's supported by stronger structural free cash flow, and that comes from volume growth, and that comes from lower unit OpEx, right? We're working both of those hard. As our plans come to fruition, that just supports further dividend growth in the future. We had a significant increase earlier this year. As we go through time, we'll continue to look at that in the context of our business, and hope to show continued growth and, very importantly, sustainable growth.
Doug Leggate
Managing Director and Senior Research Analyst, Wolfe Research
Right around CAD 35 is the answer, Dan, for the current level?
Dan Lyons
SVP, Finance and Administration, and Controller, Imperial Oil
Yeah. Well, that's the most recently disclosed level in our investor day. When we do our next investor day, we'll put out the most current number. That's a good ballpark number to work with, certainly.
Doug Leggate
Managing Director and Senior Research Analyst, Wolfe Research
Tremendous. Thanks very much indeed, guys. I appreciate you taking my questions.
Brad Corson
Chairman, President, and CEO, Imperial Oil
Thanks, Doug.
Operator
This does conclude today's question and answer session. I would now like to turn the call back to Peter Shaw for any additional or closing remarks.
Peter Shaw
VP and Investor Relations, Imperial Oil
Thank you. On behalf of the management team, I would like to thank everyone for joining us this morning. As always, if anyone has further questions, please don't hesitate to reach out to the investor relations team, and we'd be happy to answer those questions. With that, we thank you very much, and we hope you enjoy the rest of your day and the weekend. Thank you.
Operator
This does conclude today's call. Thank you for your participation. You may now disconnect.
