Operator
Good day, and welcome to the Imperial Oil Q4 Earnings Call. At this time, I would like to turn the conference over to Dave Hughes, VP Investor Relations. Please go ahead.
Dave Hughes
VP, Investor Relations, Imperial Oil
Thank you very much, and good morning, everybody. Welcome to our Q4 earnings call. Here today are Brad Corson, Chairman, President and CEO; Dan Lyons, Senior Vice President, Finance and Administration; Simon Younger, Senior Vice President of the Upstream; Jon Wetmore, Vice President of the Downstream; and Sherri Evers, Vice President of Commercial and Corporate Development. I'm just gonna start with a cautionary statement. Today's comments include reference to non-GAAP financial measures. Definitions and reconciliations of these measures can be found in attachment six of our most recent press release and are available on our website with a link to this conference call. Today's comments may also contain forward-looking information. Any forward-looking information is not a guarantee of future performance, and actual future performance and operating results can vary materially depending on a number of factors and assumptions.
Forward-looking information and the risk factors and assumptions described in further detail in our Q4 earnings release that we issued this morning, as well as our most recent Form 10-K. All of these documents are available on SEDAR, EDGAR, and on our website, so please refer to those. After Brad's opening remarks, as usual, Dan will give a financial update, and then we'll go back to Brad for an operational update, and we'll follow with all of the Q&A session. With that, I'm happy to turn it over to Brad for his opening remarks.
Brad Corson
Chairman, President, and CEO, Imperial Oil
All right. Thanks, Dave. Good morning, everybody, and happy New Year. Welcome to our Q4 earnings call. I hope you're all doing well and your new year is off to a good start. As we close out 2022 reporting, I'm pleased to share another very strong quarter for Imperial in what has been a standout year for us, both financially and operationally. Our Downstream continued to deliver exceptional operating and financial performance in the Q4, while Kearl tied a quarterly production record and Cold Lake and Syncrude continued to deliver strong production results as well. It's especially satisfying to see this level of operating performance in a year where commodity prices were so supportive, which in turn allowed us to maximize value for our shareholders. Looking back on the full year, we are closing the books on what was the best year in the company's history.
A stark contrast to the challenges we faced just two years ago at the depths of COVID. In 2022, we set numerous records, both operating and financial. We delivered record earnings and cash flow, as well as record shareholder returns underpinned by a 63% increase to our dividend and over CAD 6 billion in share buybacks. Operationally, we continue to see Kearl deliver new daily and quarterly best evers, further supporting our confidence in achieving 280,000 barrels per day gross by 2024. Cold Lake delivered production at the high end of the upwardly revised guidance range, and Syncrude had a best ever production year supported by the interconnecting bi-directional pipelines. In the Downstream, our refining assets achieved best ever utilization, allowing us to maximize products available to the market.
In addition to these performance achievements, we continue to reinvest in the business, and we successfully advanced multiple accretive capital projects, such as completion of the Sarnia Products Pipeline, which improves our ability to supply refined products to markets in Ontario. We also made significant progress on our commitments to sustainability and decarbonization, including a decision to invest in Canada's largest renewable diesel manufacturing facility at Strathcona, material progress on the Pathways initiative, and establishing a corporate-wide net zero goal. We'll talk more about many of these achievements over the next several minutes. The overall macro environment remained positive through the year. While commodity prices did soften somewhat in Q4, they remain quite strong due to global effects of ongoing supply challenges, growing demand, and ongoing geopolitical events.
Our unrelenting focus on safety and reliability enables our strong operating performance in this environment and continues to underpin our strong financial results. Over the next few minutes, Dan and I will detail the results of what was a very strong quarter. Now let's review the Q4 results. Earnings for the quarter were just over CAD 1.7 billion, and our cash from operating activities was almost CAD 2.8 billion. Another strong operating quarter, including Kearl matching its best ever production quarter and the Downstream setting a utilization record, coupled with continued strong commodity fundamentals, most notably robust diesel crack spreads, supported these strong results.
Full year 2022 saw record operating performance across our assets, which played a large part in generating full-year earnings of over CAD 7.3 billion and operating cash flow of almost CAD 10.5 billion, the strongest financial results in Imperial's history. These strong financial results come with increased royalty and tax contributions to the provincial and federal governments, providing economic benefits for all Canadians. We achieved total upstream production of 441,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day in the quarter, reflecting continued strong, and in some cases, record-setting performance across our upstream assets, which I'll talk more about in just a few minutes. I would also note that Northern Alberta experienced another significant cold weather event in December, and I'm pleased to say we managed through that just fine.
A huge thank you to the efforts of our operating teams who continue to work safely and diligently to provide reliable energy supply to the market. In the Downstream, we saw another outstanding quarter. Our refinery utilization in the quarter was 101%, marking the Q2 in a row with utilization at or above 100%, and also the highest quarterly utilization we have seen in the company's history, surpassing the previous record set just last quarter. This also contributed to the highest annual utilization in the company's history. Given the current commodity price environment driven by external supply challenges we've talked about previously, this level of performance is delivering tremendous value. The Q4 also saw us continue to maximize shareholder returns.
We completed the accelerated NCIB in October and successfully executed our second substantial issuer bid in 2022, returning CAD 1.5 billion of cash to our shareholders in December on top of the CAD 2.5 billion SIB completed back in June. This was in addition to CAD 211 million in dividends paid in the quarter, for a total of CAD 851 million for the year. Altogether, this represents over CAD 7 billion of cash returned to shareholders in 2022, the highest level of returns in Imperial's history. Finally, this morning we declared a dividend of CAD 0.44 per share, payable 1st April 2023.
I can assure you that in 2023, we are maintaining our core strategy of optimizing our existing asset base to drive maximum shareholder value, a strategy that will allow us to continue to focus on returning cash to our shareholders. With that, I'll pass things over to Dan.
Daniel Lyons
SVP, Finance and Administration, Imperial Oil
Thanks, Brad. Starting with financial results for the full year, we recorded net income of over CAD 7.3 billion, as Brad mentioned, our highest on record, and an increase of around CAD 4.9 billion from 2021, driven mainly by higher realizations in the Upstream and higher margins in the Downstream, underpinned by strong operational performance. Looking at the Q4, our net income of CAD 1.727 billion was up CAD 914 million when compared to the Q4 of 2021, primarily driven by higher margins in the Downstream. Looking sequentially, our Q4 net income of CAD 1.727 billion is down CAD 304 million from Q3. We're down around CAD 100 million when excluding the XTO sale that occurred in Q3.
This reflects lower bitumen realizations in the Upstream, partly offset by improved Upstream and Downstream volumes. Now looking at each business line, the Upstream reported net income of CAD 531 million in Q4, down CAD 455 million from Q3. We're down CAD 250 million when we exclude the impact of the XTO sale, driven primarily by lower realizations, partly offset by higher volumes. The Downstream's net income was CAD 1.188 billion, up CAD 176 million from Q3, mainly reflecting higher volumes from achieving record refinery utilization rates in Q4, including continued strong distillate production. Finally, our Chemicals business continued to demonstrate reliable operational performance with net income of CAD 41 million in Q4, down from our Q3 net income of CAD 54 million.
Moving on to cash flow. In Q4, we generated nearly CAD 2.8 billion in cash flows from operating activities, down around CAD 300 million from Q3, bringing our full-year cash flows from operating activities to around CAD 10.5 billion, up over CAD 5 billion from last year, reflecting strong earnings and favorable working capital impacts. Free cash flow for the quarter was CAD 2.3 billion, bringing our full-year free cash flow to about CAD 9.9 billion, CAD 5.4 billion higher than last year, primarily driven by the increase in cash flows from operations that I just mentioned, and by the cash received from the XTO sale in Q3. Total cash tax payments in 2022 were around CAD 400 million.
As previously discussed, we will be making a 2022 income tax catch up payment in Q1, and we anticipate that this catch up payment will be on the order of CAD 2.1 billion, which is lower than our previous forecast of around CAD 2.5 billion. Going forward, under current market conditions, we expect to be tax paying in 2023 on a current basis and therefore expect to make regular tax installment payments throughout the year at a tax rate of about 24%. Finally, we ended the year with over CAD 3.7 billion of cash on hand, up CAD 173 million from Q3. Discussing CapEx, capital expenditures totaled CAD 488 million in Q4 and just under CAD 1.5 billion for the full year.
In the Downstream, 2022 spending included completing the Sarnia Products Pipeline early in the year and progressing our renewable diesel project at Strathcona, which has been mentioned earlier, has now received FID and is planned to start up in early 2025. In the Upstream, 2022 spending focused on smaller projects to sustain and grow production at both Kearl and Cold Lake, as well as larger projects like the In-Pit Tailings Project at Kearl and the SA-SAGD Grand Rapids project at Cold Lake. As noted in our full year 2023 guidance issued in December, we plan to complete the Grand Rapids project on an accelerated basis by the end of this year, about one year ahead of schedule.
This accelerated schedule increased our 2022 CapEx by about CAD 100 million relative to our 2022 guidance of CAD 1.4 billion. Shifting to shareholder distributions, we continue to demonstrate our long-standing commitment to return cash to shareholders. A reliable and growing dividend is fundamental to our cash distribution strategy, and as Brad noted this morning, we declared a Q1 dividend of CAD 0.44 per share payable in April. We have increased our annual dividend payment for 28 consecutive years, and this year we increased our quarterly dividend payment by 63% year over year from CAD 0.27 per share in Q1 2022 to CAD 0.44 per share paid in Q1 2023.
We completed our most recent accelerated NCIB program with purchases of over CAD 400 million in October, and we completed our second substantial issuer bid in December, repurchasing CAD 1.5 billion in outstanding shares. As Brad noted, in total, throughout the course of the year, we completed record shareholder returns of over CAD 7.2 billion, including CAD 851 million in dividends and share repurchases of about CAD 6.4 billion. These share repurchases represent over 90 million shares and almost 14% of our shares outstanding. Now I'll turn it back to Brad to discuss our operational performance.
Brad Corson
Chairman, President, and CEO, Imperial Oil
All right. Thanks, Dan. Now let's talk about the operating results for the quarter. Upstream production for the quarter averaged 441,000 oil-equivalent barrels per day, which is up 11,000 barrels per day versus Q3 2022, but 4,000 barrels per day lower versus Q4 2021. The drop versus Q4 2021 is more than accounted for by the absence of XTO volumes in Q4 2022, which totaled 15,000 oil-equivalent barrels per day. Adjusting for the sale of XTO, production actually increased by 11,000 oil-equivalent barrels per day versus Q4 2021.
The increase versus Q3 reflects continued strong operating performance at Kearl and Cold Lake, as well as an excellent quarter for Syncrude following completion in Q3 of its planned turnaround. For the full year, upstream production was 416,000 oil equivalent barrels per day. Strength in commodity prices was a key part of the story throughout 2022. I noted on our Q3 call that the WTI/WCS differential was coming under some pressure in the quarter, resulting in a widening of around CAD 6 per barrel versus Q2. We saw this continue in Q4, with the WTI/WCS spread widening further by over CAD 7 per barrel to a level of approximately CAD 26 per barrel.
I would note, however, that we've seen a modest narrowing of the spread so far in Q1 to around $23 per barrel and expect further narrowing as the year progresses. I would also note that we continue to see strong diesel crack spreads, which provides a counter to the wide crude differentials and highlights the value of integration between our upstream and downstream. Additionally, our downstream directly benefits from lower prices on the heavy crudes we process, especially when coupled with the higher diesel crack spreads I mentioned. Further, Syncrude synthetic product commanded a strong premium in Q4. All of this adds up to very robust cash generation for our downstream business. Once again, underscores the strong value of integration that we realize. Now let's move on and talk a bit about Kearl.
Kearl's production in Q4 averaged 284,000 barrels per day gross, which was up 13,000 barrels per day versus Q3, and was up 14,000 barrels per day from Q4 2021. This Q4 production is in line with Kearl's previous best quarter, which was Q4 2020, and contributed to the best H2 of production in the asset's history. As I mentioned earlier, the team was able to successfully manage through a significant cold weather event in December. This is notable at Kearl, given some of the challenges we faced in the first quarter of last year due to weather, and reflects the positive impact of enhanced winter operating practices that were developed and implemented after the January 2022 weather issues.
The strong H2 demonstrates fully recovering from the challenges of Q1 and brings full-year production at Kearl to 242,000 barrels per day gross. Its further demonstration of Kearl's strong H2 and finish to the year. On 29th December 2022, the asset yet again broke its record for daily production, delivering an all-time high of around 360,000 barrels per day gross. Yes, that starts with a three. We are seeing strong production for this time of year as we move into 2023, with January month-to-date production at Kearl at around 265,000 barrels per day. I recognize that winter is far from over, but this is a great start. Finally, turning to operating costs.
We saw a slight increase of just under $2 per barrel versus Q3 to just under $27 per barrel all-in, driven partially by higher energy requirements and incremental maintenance in support of our winter operating strategy. Given a number of structural cost reduction initiatives we are working on, we continue to target sustainable unit operating costs at or below $20 per barrel at Kearl. What a year 2022 was it for Cold Lake. An ongoing focus on production optimization and reliability resulted in exceptional full-year production levels, with Cold Lake averaging 144,000 barrels per day, which was at the high end of our revised guidance and represents its highest full-year production since 2018.
Production for Q4 averaged 141,000 barrels per day, which was down 9,000 barrels per day from Q3 and just slightly below Q4 2021. This is also the fifth consecutive quarter with production at or above 140,000 barrels per day. We're continuing to invest in Cold Lake. We are in the early stages of the Leming field redevelopment, and as we mentioned with our 2023 guidance release, we have accelerated Grand Rapids phase one, now expecting to start up later this year.
Imperial's share of Syncrude production for the quarter averaged 87,000 barrels per day, which was up 8,000 barrels per day from Q4 2021 due to lower unplanned downtime and up 25,000 barrels per day from Q3 2022 following the completion in Q3 of the asset's major plant turnaround. Throughout 2022, the interconnect pipeline between Syncrude and Suncor averaged about 3,000 barrels per day of export sales, enabling Syncrude to achieve record annual production of 77,000 barrels per day Imperial's share. In 2023, Suncor, the operator, will continue to focus on the implementation of a significant transition plan. The integration of systems, processes, and people remains a high priority and is largely on plan. We expect that the realization of synergy benefits will continue to grow with further integration in 2023.
Now let's move on and talk about the Downstream. In Q4, we refined an average of 433,000 barrels per day, which was up 7,000 barrels a day versus Q3 and up 17,000 barrels per day versus Q4 2021, reflecting continued strong operating performance and minimal planned turnaround activity. Refinery utilization was exceptional at 101%, marking the second quarter in a row with utilization at or above 100% and also the highest utilization in company history. Another outstanding quarter and a great credit to our refinery teams who remain focused on reliability and optimization to deliver these results.
On a full-year basis, our refineries individually achieved records, bringing total full-year throughput to 418,000 barrels per day, which represents a utilization of 98%, which was also the highest in company history and well above our annual guidance of 92% to 94%. Something we talked about before that still may not be fully appreciated is the flexibility we have in our Downstream operations, allowing us to adjust our product slates to capture market opportunities, such as what we are seeing with diesel right now. In fact, our refining network was able to deliver record distillate production at our existing assets, allowing us to capture maximum value from the strong diesel margins throughout the year. As we have noted before, 2022 was a relatively light year for planned maintenance and turnarounds at our refineries.
As we communicated in our 2023 guidance announcement back in December, 2023 will be a more typical year for planned maintenance in the Downstream. Finally, with respect to our refining business, I am very pleased and proud to note that late last week, we announced that we had made the final investment decision to develop what will be Canada's largest renewable diesel manufacturing facility at our Strathcona refinery. This unit will produce more than one billion liters of renewable diesel annually, primarily from locally sourced feedstocks, and could help reduce greenhouse gas emissions by about three million metric tons per year. Work is already underway, and we expect renewable diesel production to start in early 2025. We continue to expect a strong return for that project, particularly as we've added accretive rail logistics scope to access high-value markets.
The updated concept select for this capital investment is CAD 720 million. This current higher cost reflects three main drivers. First, as we shared with our December guidance press release, we've added rail logistics scope, which will allow us to access higher-value markets for the products. Second, we refined preliminary directional estimates around project development activities for things like construction requirements. Third, we've seen some cost increase for materials such as steel, as you might expect, given the inflationary environment we're in. Most importantly, even with these higher costs, we are still seeing a very similar strong return, and this is primarily because of the highly accretive nature of the added rail logistics scope, but also further refinement of overall economic value.
This project is another example of our focus on reinvesting in our business with an eye to the energy transition and future competitiveness, and doing so in a way that creates value for our shareholders. Now, petroleum product sales in the quarter were 487,000 barrels per day, which is up 3,000 barrels per day versus Q3 and down 9,000 barrels per day versus Q4 2021. Demand for all products has remained stable, with motor gasoline at around 95% of 2019 levels, diesel at essentially 100%, and jet actually exceeding 2019 levels in Q4 at around 115%. We continued to see a positive downstream margin environment in Q4, and though we did see some weakening of motor gasoline margins, they remain within normal historical bands.
Diesel margins remained extremely strong. These dynamics are driven by a number of factors, including low product inventories, and a global shortfall for diesel fuel. That brings us to chemicals. This business continued to deliver strong results with earnings of CAD 41 million in Q4, which was down CAD 13 million from Q3 and down CAD 23 million from Q4 2021, primarily driven by lower margins. This brings full-year chemical earnings to CAD 204 million, another very healthy year for our advantaged chemical business, despite being in a down cycle for chemicals, and once again highlighting the value of having this business fully integrated with our Sarnia refinery. As always, I'd like to wrap up by highlighting a couple other items of note, particularly as it pertains to our ongoing commitment to improving sustainability and reducing our overall environmental footprint.
First, as we continue to make progress on advancing the lower carbon solutions that will support our journey towards net zero, Imperial has now established a company-wide goal to achieve net zero emissions for Scope One and Scope Two by 2050 across all of its operated assets, not just oil sands. We expect to achieve this through collaboration with government and other industry partners, successful technology development and deployment, and supportive fiscal and regulatory frameworks. This announcement builds on our previously announced Net Zero goal for operated oil sands as part of the Pathways Alliance initiative, as well as the company's 2030 emission intensity reduction goal for operated oil sands.
I'd also like to highlight that the Pathways Alliance entered into an agreement with the Government of Alberta on pore space, enabling the alliance to begin more detailed work evaluating the storage zone by using test wells to get a full understanding of the characteristics of the geology in the hub region. This progress is very encouraging and marks a major milestone in our efforts to progress our plan to help Canada meet its climate goals and ensure our country becomes a preferred global supplier of responsibly produced oil. There is tremendous amount of activity going on with the Pathways Alliance.
In October, the alliance communicated an expected total investment for the first phase of the project at around CAD 24 billion, and initial efforts under this phase are already underway on activities such as feasibility studies, environmental assessments, and early engineering work. In closing, another excellent quarter to finish off an excellent year. We saw high reliability in our operations across the board, setting a number of operating records across our assets and allowing us to continue to benefit from the strong business environment and to deliver very strong financial results. We returned over CAD 2.1 billion to our shareholders in the quarter via our reliable and growing dividend and the successful execution of our second substantial issuer bid. This contributed to shareholder returns for the full year in excess of CAD 7 billion.
We continue to make progress on our commitment to lower our carbon footprint. In addition to the continued progress on Pathways, we announced a decision to move forward with renewable diesel investment at our Strathcona refinery as well as a corporate-wide net zero by 2050 goal. We announced our intention to accelerate our deployment of next-generation in situ technology with the Grand Rapids project at Cold Lake. All in all, a fantastic year for Imperial. Our continued focus on our strategic priorities, those being continually improving reliability, and investing in high-value, opportunistic growth opportunities, generated tremendous value for Imperial. A focus on shareholder returns resulted in the highest level of cash in our history being returned to our shareholders. As we look ahead to 2023, I'm viewing the year with a high level of optimism and excitement.
We are coming off the strongest year in the company's history, and with our ongoing focus on safe and reliable operations that drove our 2022 performance, I fully expect the company to deliver another excellent year. As always, I'd like to thank you once again for your continued interest and support. Now we'll move to the Q&A session, so I'll pass it back to Dave.
Dave Hughes
VP, Investor Relations, Imperial Oil
Okay, thanks, Brad and Dan. We're gonna go to the Q&A now. I would ask you to please limit yourself to one question and a follow-up. With that, operator, could you please go to the first question?
Operator
Yes, thank you. If you would like to ask a question, please signal by pressing star one on your telephone keypad. If you're using a speakerphone, please make sure your mute function is turned off to allow your signal to reach our equipment. Again, please press star one to ask a question. We will go first to Greg Pardy with RBC Capital.
Greg Pardy
Managing Director and Head of Global Energy Research, RBC Capital Markets
Yeah, thanks. Good morning, and thanks for the detailed rundown. Brad, I was wondering if we could just dig back into Kearl a little bit. Not so much the production rates, which have been strong, but perhaps your comment around the weatherproofing that was undertaken last year and that prepared you as well for the cold weather we went through in December. Could you be more specific in terms of the actions that you took?
Brad Corson
Chairman, President, and CEO, Imperial Oil
Yeah. Thanks for the question, Greg, and Happy New Year. You know, it's really kind of a combination of several initiatives that encompass operating practices and procedures, establishing appropriate limits on certain metrics that we use to monitor our business. We also invested in some equipment upgrades and further monitoring. It's really a wide range of things, Greg. You know, when we put all those things together, it is about ensuring that we've got the right procedures in place, we've got the right equipment in place, we've got the right monitoring of extreme conditions, and we have contingency plans on how to react to those extreme conditions.
It's difficult to be kind of more precise in the limited amount of time because it's a lot of, you know, it's a lot of very discrete activities. Something that the team spent really, you know, several months in really kind of reassessing on all of the root causes that contributed to the downtime last year and making sure we understood that root cause and taking appropriate mitigations. Hope that's helpful.
Greg Pardy
Managing Director and Head of Global Energy Research, RBC Capital Markets
Yeah, no, it is. Understood. Hopefully we'd learn a bit more of that on your Investor Day back in April. But maybe just the follow-up question, completely shifting gears, and perhaps a question for Dan comes back to, you know, you did two SIBs last year. You got, what, CAD 3+ billion of cash on hand. Your cash tax is smaller. Your NCIB is exhausted. I mean, we've got nothing in for repurchases in H1, which we know is off the mark. I'm just wondering what your appetite is for another SIB and just generally how you're thinking about that.
Daniel Lyons
SVP, Finance and Administration, Imperial Oil
Yeah, Greg. You know, I would say, look, our policy or sort of philosophy on returning surplus cash to shareholders has been unchanged for a long time. To the extent we continue to generate, the market gives us and our operational performance gives us surplus cash, we're gonna return that to shareholders. You know, what'll happen H1 of this year, it's gonna depend on market conditions, obviously. You know, if we can, I don't know if you pointed out, but we can't renew our NCIB until, you know, late June, essentially, call it 1st July.
Could there be a return before that? It's possible. You know, we have not made any decisions. We don't know where our cash is gonna be. As a broad principle, when we generate surplus cash, we will return it to shareholders. You know, our go-to has been the NCIB, and if that's not available or exhausted, it's been the SIB. As we've said before, you know, we're not wedded to that. There's other things like, you know, special dividends, but the SIB seems to be what the vast majority of our shareholders prefer relative to special dividends. That remains our go-to at this point. We'll see. We'll see what happens. We'll see what the market gives us.
Greg Pardy
Managing Director and Head of Global Energy Research, RBC Capital Markets
Okay. Understood. Thank you both.
Brad Corson
Chairman, President, and CEO, Imperial Oil
Thanks, Greg.
Operator
We'll go next to Doug. Oh, I'm sorry. We'll go next to Doug Leggate with Bank of America.
Doug Leggate
Managing Director and Head of Global Oil & Gas Equity. Research, Bank of America
Well, thanks, everyone. Hi, Brad. Happy New Year, and to all your team. I wonder if I could ask a couple questions, one operational and one about my favorite topic as Dan knows well, is dividend policy. First, operationally, your refining performance was, compared to your peers, is quite extraordinary. Obviously your distillate yield is a little higher. You've got some exposure to WCS. I wonder if you could kind of walk us through how you see the outlook for your refining business, because it looks like there's been some channel changes in terms of how you've been able to maximize margins, particularly, I guess, in the Northeast during Q4. Anything you would call out on the strength of that refining performance is my first question, and then I'll have my follow-up, if that's okay.
Brad Corson
Chairman, President, and CEO, Imperial Oil
Okay. Yeah. Thanks, Doug, and Happy New Year to you as well. You know, when we look at the refining business, it is very much around maximizing value of our products, driven by kind of our operating envelopes at each of our three refineries, coupled with you know, the commodity pricing and the crack spreads that are available to us. You know, what we saw late in the year, Q3, Q4, was these extremely robust diesel crack spreads and you know, that was very motivational to us you know, both operationally and financially to maximize diesel. So a great credit to the team.
You know, they optimized around their operating envelopes at each of our three refineries, set records around levels of distillate that we produced, and you know that had two beneficial effects. I mean, one, it put more product on the market at a time when you know the market needed it, and it also allowed us to maximize value from that strategy. As we look into you know the first part of this year, we're continuing to see you know a lot of strength in the diesel side of the business. So the teams are continuing to optimize around that. You know, we'll just continue to assess that as the year goes forward.
It really does speak to, you know, the capabilities of our assets, where they can, you know, shift between diesel, jet, and motor gasoline, you know, at the margins, and allows us to maximize value.
Doug Leggate
Managing Director and Head of Global Oil & Gas Equity. Research, Bank of America
Okay. Nothing unusual in the quarter then other than just optimization basically, which is a go-forward staple, I suppose.
Brad Corson
Chairman, President, and CEO, Imperial Oil
Yeah. I think that's right. Continuing to optimize around the market conditions that we see.
Doug Leggate
Managing Director and Head of Global Oil & Gas Equity. Research, Bank of America
Okay. That's a good answer. Anyway, thank you. We'll keep an eye on it going forward. Might have some upside risk to street numbers if that performance continues. My follow-up is kind of a hypothetical, I guess. I realize Greg asked about the SIB. I wanna ask about the balance between the buybacks, which obviously have some limitations, and thinking back to the share price response to when you raised your dividend last October. Because it seems to us that long life assets, you know, high reliability long life assets like yourselves with tremendous cash dividend cover, you get paid on a dividend discount model, and your dividend growth potential remains quite extraordinary compared to your peer group.
I guess my question is, how should we think about that balance between continuing to go after things like an SIB versus stepping up the sustainable dividend payout? Because let's say a 10% buyback means your starting point is a 10% dividend growth. How should we think about that balance? I'll leave it there. Thank you.
Brad Corson
Chairman, President, and CEO, Imperial Oil
Yeah. Thanks for that question, and obviously something we spend a lot of time thinking about as well. You know, I guess it starts with kind of the foundation of our capital allocation strategy, which is to provide a reliable and growing dividend. That's where we start. You know, we have a long history of that. We've been paying a reliable dividend to our shareholders for over 100 years. We've grown that dividend year on year for the last 28 years. So that is core to our strategy, and that's gonna continue to be the first place we go as we think about shareholder distributions. We certainly supplement that with NCIBs and SIBs to be, you know, reflective of, you know, current market conditions and cash flow generation. But the foundation is this reliable and growing dividend.
You know, you've seen us grow it quite significantly over the last couple of years. You know, we see that there is potential for further growth in the dividend, but we are always gonna be conscious of the sustainability of that dividend. You know, when we take a decision, you know, whether it's a small growth or a large growth, it's with a lot of consideration to what does the future look like and, you know, ensuring that that dividend is sustainable over a wide range of scenarios. Not just the current market we're in, but recognizing we are in a commodity market that has a cyclical nature to it. You know, whereas we're all benefiting from, you know, CAD 80 crude today, it wasn't that long ago that was CAD 40 or below.
You know, certainly the potential is that somewhere in the future we'll return to lower levels of commodity pricing. We wanna make sure that that dividend is sustainable. We're gonna continue to evaluate on that basis. Mathematically and mechanically, you are exactly right though. As we buy back shares and we reduce the outstanding share count, that gives us flexibility to raise the dividend, but not really raise the cash outlay for the dividend because it applies to fewer shares. You know, as Dan just described, you know, we bought back almost 15% of the shares. That gives us significant flexibility in that regard. You know, as we go forward over the next couple of quarters, we'll be continuing to evaluate what's the appropriate strategy to return cash to shareholders.
Again, that strategy starts with growing the dividend.
Doug Leggate
Managing Director and Head of Global Oil & Gas Equity. Research, Bank of America
Appreciate the answers, guys. Thanks so much.
Brad Corson
Chairman, President, and CEO, Imperial Oil
Thanks, Doug.
Operator
We'll go next to Dennis Fong with CIBC World Markets.
Dennis Fong
Institutional Equity Research covering Energy Infrastructure,, CIBC World Markets
Hi, excuse me, good morning, and thanks for taking my questions. The first one, maybe I wouldn't mind starting, you guys have focused on optimizing the existing assets. That was in your opening comments, as well as the acceleration of the Grand Rapids project. I wanted to hopefully pick your brain a little bit about, maybe the pipeline of additional projects that can possibly drive, we'll call it upside in terms of upstream production, as well as helping kind of moderate cost inflation or even lowering unit operating costs amongst your various assets.
Brad Corson
Chairman, President, and CEO, Imperial Oil
Yeah, thanks for that question, Dennis. We do have a suite of project opportunities, you know, across our assets. You know, it sounds like your question is mostly focused on the Upstream. Although I would just maybe first note, you know, what we're doing in the Downstream with the renewable diesel project, you know, 20,000 barrels per day growth to the Strathcona asset, you know, which is slightly above 200,000 barrels a day base today. 10% increase right there alone. That's on the Downstream. Back to the Upstream, you know, we have now for several years laid out this vision at Kearl to grow to 280,000 barrels per day, we continue to make material progress towards that.
You know, that's with multiple project initiatives, brownfield, high return projects. As you know, we have now firmed up our guidance and commitment that by next year, 2024, we will reach 280,000 barrels a day at Kearl. We're continuing to evaluate further opportunities to move us you know even beyond 280,000 barrels a day. We're not ready to talk about those details yet because you know the asset teams are still kind of refining that work program. When we get to Investor Day, we'll start to lay out you know kinda some more details on that.
At Cold Lake, you know, you've heard us talk about Grand Rapids phase one, acceleration of that now for a startup to the end of this year. We haven't talked a lot about it on these calls, but in parallel to the Grand Rapids project, we've also initiated a Leming redevelopment project at kind of the original field at Cold Lake. That project is about a year behind Grand Rapids and a little bit smaller. You know, it's more like eight to nine thousand barrels a day, but it does represent another growth opportunity for us. We're continuing to do kind of infill drilling across Cold Lake, and that's contributing to the higher volumes, you know, that we saw last year.
We've got a whole pipeline of additional solvent deployment opportunities at Grand Rapids, I mean, at Cold Lake. You know, you've seen us deploy SAGD, SA-SAGD. We're continuing to explore future generations of opportunities that will allow us to not only grow production, but do that in a lower-cost way, and also, quite importantly, with lower emissions intensity. All that work is going on. Further out, of course, in the pipeline, we've got Aspen. You know, before we're ready to progress that, we're doing some more work on solvent technologies that we think have the potential to further reduce the capital costs, the operating costs, and significantly lower the emissions associated with that project as well. We've got a technology that we've proven in the lab.
We want to further validate it with a field pilot test, and so we're progressing plans for that. Really a strong pipeline of opportunities there. Of course, you know, at Syncrude, we've talked before about, you know, the work we're doing with Suncor, the operator, and the other owners around how can we generate further value from that asset. Of course, the bi-directional pipelines has been a very positive contributor. But we're continuing to look for other ways to increase reliability and productive capability out of that asset as well.
Dennis Fong
Institutional Equity Research covering Energy Infrastructure,, CIBC World Markets
Great. That was a very fulsome answer. My follow-up here is more on the Downstream side. I guess expectations for some of your peers going into Q1 suggest some level of downtime, just on the back of extreme weather we saw going into the end of 2022. Do you mind talking to your ability to further take advantage of some of these increased margins that we're seeing in Q1, as well as the ability of Imperial to capture value out of the commodity price volatility that we're seeing, both from an oil side as well as a product side space?
Brad Corson
Chairman, President, and CEO, Imperial Oil
Yeah. Thanks for the question. You know, I am pleased to be able to talk at this point, you know, of a very different result than from the weather than we saw, you know, a year ago when, of course, we did have some challenges at Kearl. For this year, despite those weather challenges, you know, across our assets, both Upstream and Downstream, including all three of our refineries, you know, we've managed quite well through those extreme weather conditions, very high reliability. You know, we haven't experienced the downtime that others have, so we're quite fortunate in that regard and a great credit to our operating organization.
What that allows us to do is, as you made reference, you know, we continue to find ourselves in a very strong margin environment. That high reliability, you know, coupled with those high margins, will allow us to to generate significant value. On top of that, though, you know, as others experience downtime, you know, and we never wish that on our competitors, but, you know, it's just a reality of the situation they find themselves in, then that sometimes opens up opportunities for us to, on kind of a one-off basis, supply some of their customers in the market. It generates an opportunity for us to even increase our product sales beyond kind of our normal levels.
You know, again, our teams are working diligently to see how to, you know, best supply, you know, customers with products and how to do that in the most economic way.
Dennis Fong
Institutional Equity Research covering Energy Infrastructure,, CIBC World Markets
Great. Thanks, Brad. I'll turn it back.
Brad Corson
Chairman, President, and CEO, Imperial Oil
Great. Thanks, Dennis.
Operator
We'll go next to Menno Hulshof with TD Securities.
Menno Hulshof
Managing Director, Institutional Equity Research, TD Securities
Thanks, good morning, everyone. I'll start with Strathcona Renewable Diesel. You clearly had enough confidence in the economics to FID last week. Given the cost and the scope increase, could we get your thoughts on sort of the range of outcomes on project returns or even the project hurdle? Finally, where do things stand in terms of signing of feedstock supply agreements?
Brad Corson
Chairman, President, and CEO, Imperial Oil
Yeah. Thanks for those questions, Menno. You know, I mean, first, I would just say, you know, we don't normally talk about individual rates of returns on projects like this, although, you know, I can assure you it is a very robust return. It's double-digit return, and it competes very well with other projects in our portfolio that are competing for capital, and hence the reason we took it to FID.
I have with me, you know, Jon Wetmore, who's the VP of our Downstream and has been, you know, directly involved with this project from the outset and bringing a lot of leadership to moving it along kind of through the decision process, you know, so maybe I'll turn it to him to talk maybe a little bit more about cost and then also kind of the some of those supply contracts.
J.R. Wetmore
VP of the Downstream, Jon
Thanks, Brad. It's Jon Wetmore here, Menno. Thanks for the question. We did see some cost increases on the project, and I think Brad talked about that in his opening remarks. Really, they're driven by the fact that we've seen some amount of inflationary pressures in the project's labor and materials. A little bit of constructability issues as well, as we're knitting together some catalysts that are third-party catalysts with our highly advantaged dewaxing catalyst that's proprietary to ExxonMobil technology. When we did that, the last layer of cost that we saw come into this is really around added logistics and some very high return additions to the project scope. They come in the way of us looking at where we wanna sell the renewable diesel across Western Canada and potentially into the US.
The return on all those added logistics and that last layer of scope that we added is incredibly strong, and it really nullified the impact of all those cost increases on the project's rate of return. We're really happy and had a good review with our board here about reviewing the project's rate of return as being neutral even after that CAD 200 million of cost was added. We are, you know, very strong, as Brad said, competes very well with the rest of our portfolio. There's nothing about the fact that it's a renewable diesel project or driven by regulatory compliance that in any way suggests that its rate of return is below our portfolio. Very, very competitive and at the top of our portfolio.
In terms of feedstock, you know, we're working diligently around that with some of the best in industry that provide vegetable oils. We're looking at a variety of different sources so that we're insulated to a little bit of everything, from weather conditions to local sourcing challenges. You know, we're learning a lot about the industry as we go, and we've got a lot more left to learn. You know, we'll be humble and say that there's a lot of the whole area of the vegetable oil supply chain that we've got to develop and add to this project. But we've got our fingers into a lot of opportunity there. We feel very good that all that will be in play in the first year of the project startup.
You know, we'll continue to develop some sophistication, added sophistication around those feedstock deals as time comes.
Menno Hulshof
Managing Director, Institutional Equity Research, TD Securities
Terrific. Yeah, that was super helpful, Jon. Maybe I'll follow up with the CCUS question since you're the first Pathways member to report. Pretty standard question. How are things looking in terms of resolution of discussions with the feds on additional incentives? Is it possible that we see something with the announcement of the budget, or do you think it's a bit further out than that?
Brad Corson
Chairman, President, and CEO, Imperial Oil
Yeah, thanks for that question. I'd you know kinda start my response by just noting that, you know, we continue to make great progress on kind of the whole breadth of the Pathways activities, including, you know, as I put in some of my earlier remarks, you know, progress on the pipeline, the main trunk line design, you know, environmental studies are underway in the field. We're continuing as individual companies to work on the capture side of each of the, you know, many projects that will feed captured carbon into the pipeline, and of course, great progress on the pore space award from the provincial government. On the federal side, in terms of financial support, you know, those discussions continue to be very constructive, continue to move forward.
You know, the federal government, I think, was a pace setter when they came out with, in last year's budget speech, the announcement of the 50% Investment Tax Credit, a very enabling first step for us. As time's gone on, you know, and we've seen what's happened south of the border with the US Inflation Reduction Act and some of the incentivization that's provided there, you know, it's critically important that our projects in Canada be competitive for investors that have choices to invest in either the US, Canada, or globally for that matter. The level of fiscal support is lagging, and we've always said we needed more than that 50%, so that's not a surprise.
We're also, you know, optimistic that the province will contribute to that as well. You know, it's really a tri-party discussion that's going on between the Pathways group and the federal government and the provincial government. Now whether that will get resolved or clarified further in the upcoming budget speech, I'm not sure. Again, you know, it's complex and takes, you know, a lot of important engagement to balance, you know, kind of financial priorities and applications, you know, not just for our CCUS projects, but across the broader industry and other sectors that also, you know, need access to capital. Again, you know, it's very positive.
Both governments understand what we need to move these projects forward, and they're both very supportive of moving these projects forward. I'm optimistic that, you know, if it's not in the budget speech, it'll be soon thereafter that we'll get kind of not just clarity, but resolution so we can move forward on these projects.
Menno Hulshof
Managing Director, Institutional Equity Research, TD Securities
Thanks, Brad. I'll turn it back.
Brad Corson
Chairman, President, and CEO, Imperial Oil
Thanks, Menno Hulshof.
Operator
We'll go next to Neil Mehta with Goldman Sachs.
Neil Mehta
Head of Americas Natural Resources Equity Research, Goldman Sachs
Yeah. Hey, guys. Hey, Brad. Thanks for taking the time. Two quick questions for me. One is your outlook on M&A. Brad, you spent a lot of time in M&A markets in a prior life, and what do you think Imperial's role could be in that going forward? The other is your views on WCS. We've seen a lot of volatility there. Those would be the two topics.
Brad Corson
Chairman, President, and CEO, Imperial Oil
Yeah. Okay. Thanks, Neil, and happy New Year. On M&A, you know, our position on that has not changed from what I've described in the past, which is very much centered around keeping the aperture open, looking for opportunities, you know, that are strategic and accretive for our portfolio. Part of that determination is, you know, not just what's available in the market, but also looking at our existing inventory of our own opportunities.
You know, as we've continued to evaluate M&A opportunities, and we've evaluated several, we continue to conclude that they, from a value standpoint, don't compete with projects and investment choices we already have in our portfolio, whether that be smaller projects, you know, like a Grand Rapids or like a renewable diesel that we just talked about, you know, or an even larger project like an Aspen project. We're gonna continue to evaluate how we best maximize value for our shareholders. Is it through acquisitions? Is it through continuing to advance our own, you know, deep pipeline of opportunities?
That assessment may change over time, you know, depending on, you know, what's available in the market, you know, to what degree is consolidation occurring or incentivized, you know. Again, we'll just continue to evaluate that, but no fundamental change. You know, as you saw in 2022, and I hope you'll continue to see that in 2023, we can generate a lot of value from our existing portfolio. We can return a lot of cash to shareholders. That's our first priority. The aperture is always open. On the WCS differential, you know, as-
Neil Mehta
Head of Americas Natural Resources Equity Research, Goldman Sachs
Yeah.
Brad Corson
Chairman, President, and CEO, Imperial Oil
As I've discussed in the past, you know, we saw that differential widen pretty substantially in 2022. That was driven by several external factors and not the typical egress constraints that we saw in the past. You know, that was not a material factor in the widening this last year. It was more about the release of SPR barrels that were competing, you know, with the Canadian heavies for market share. It was some refinery outages in H2 of the year that reduced demand for the heavies. It was, you know, the impact of natural gas prices and energy on refiners' ability to convert crude into products and how they, you know, what products would require less energy to produce.
All that kind of suppressed the demand for WCS, for heavy Canadian crudes, and that caused the spread to widen. Many of those effects, you know, were limited in duration. Now we're starting to see a return back to more normal situation, you know, as the SPR program, you know, was completed, refineries mostly returning back to operation. We are seeing, you know, continued growth in demand for WCS. I think that's gonna, you know, we've seen that spread already tighten a few dollars a barrel this year. You know, as we look forward, we think it'll continue to return to, you know, more normal levels.
It takes, you know, as supply-demand balances globally have been disrupted, you know, by what's happened with Russia and Ukraine and the sanctions, you know, those balances take a while to kind of restabilize. It's not, you know, a couple of weeks type thing, not even a couple of months type thing. It's often several months. I think we're now starting to see that, you know, kind of a more stable environment.
Neil Mehta
Head of Americas Natural Resources Equity Research, Goldman Sachs
Thanks, Brad.
Brad Corson
Chairman, President, and CEO, Imperial Oil
Thank you.
Operator
That does conclude the Q&A. I will turn the call back over to Dave Hughes for closing remarks.
Dave Hughes
VP, Investor Relations, Imperial Oil
Okay. Thank you. Thanks everybody for joining us this morning. If you have any further questions, please just reach out to anybody on the investor relations team here, and we're happy to continue the discussion. Thank you very much.
Operator
This does conclude today's call. You may now disconnect.
